articles.body_text:
Pope Leo is travelling to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru

Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.

The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".

It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.

At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".

"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.

"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."

On Friday Pope Leo presided over the annual memorial Mass for cardinals and bishops who have died

The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.

The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.

Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.

Father Fernando Laguna said his heart was filled with joy when the Pope's visit to Argentina was announced

"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.

"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"

The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.

'Welcome Pope Leo' reads this poster in the Argentinian church in Rome

This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.

But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.

The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.

"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.

Worshippers at Chiclayo cathedral in Peru were delighted when their former bishop became Pope in 2025

Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.

His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.

He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.

In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.

"This is how the papacy reconnects with Latin America after Francis, whose visits to the region were not always seamless," is how Professor Faggioli sees it.

He believes Pope Leo has a strong sense of the unity of the Americas as one continent. "Democracies are in trouble there, so there are so many things he can address," he suggests.

"The big question then is the United States. There's no question he wants to go. So will he travel when [President Donald] Trump is still in office? I'm sure they're thinking about this."

articles.title: Shield AI to acquire radar maker Echodyne to bust drones
articles.excerpt:
Shield AI agreed to acquire Echodyne in a $5.3 billion transaction announced Thursday — a major financial transaction that expands the prime defense contractors’ drone-warfare capabilities.

Echodyne ...
articles.body_text:
Shield AI agreed to acquire Echodyne in a $5.3 billion transaction announced Thursday — a major financial transaction that expands the prime defense contractors’ drone-warfare capabilities.

Echodyne produces next-generation, solid-state radar systems patented as Metamaterials Electronically Scanned Array (MESA) technology. Its highly advanced systems are flexible and can be easily incorporated into a wide variety of weapons and monitoring systems to detect drones, including high-energy lasers and microwave weapons.

In September, Echodyne was awarded a $250 million contract by the Defense Department’s premier national counter-drone task force, JIATF-401, to provide counter-drone technology to military forces over 36 months.

Speaking to Defense News in July, Echodyne CEO Eben Frankenberg said demand for counter-drone detecting radar is “red hot” and could grow tenfold by 2030. The company produces technology that can track small quadcopter drones and even over 1,000 objects at a time.

“There is a rush of interest globally for counter-drone,” Frankenberg told Defense News. “The Ukraine war made it obvious to everyone that drones had changed the face of warfare, but the Iran war made it obvious that everything’s at risk.”

The acquisition is a bold new move for Shield AI, which is already well-known as the maker of the X-Bat and V-Bat vertical takeoff and landing systems, or VTOL drones. The V-Bat became famous for assisting the U.S. Coast Guard in conducting reconnaissance on illicit drug trafficking at sea and enabling law enforcement to make large maritime drug busts.

The company also builds Hivemind autonomy software, which delivers AI pilots to perform multi-agent teaming and swarming across a wide range of unmanned systems, including unmanned aircraft systems, drone boats and spacecraft.

Shield AI CEO Gary Steele said the purchase of Echodyne supports the company’s aim to branch into three different areas of unmanned systems.

“We are building a new-generation defense technology company consisting of three fast-growing, high-margin, mutually supporting business units: autonomy software, autonomous systems and mission systems,” Steele said in a statement.

Frankenberg said in a statement that Shield AI’s mission complements that of Echodyne and that he expects unity of effort to multiply what both companies can deliver.

“Hundreds of customers rely on our radars to detect and track drones, protect people and infrastructure, secure borders, and ensure safe airspace operations,” Frankenberg said.

“Shield shares our view that autonomous systems can only act on what they can sense, and superior sensors lead to superior systems and outcomes,” he continued. “By joining Shield, we’re creating a company with the size and breadth to deliver even more value to our broad range of defense, government, and commercial customers around the globe.”

articles.title: 'Wipe those tears from our eyes and play like 46': Lions defense turns Jack Campbell tragedy into fuel
articles.excerpt: After the Lions’ gritty win over the Minnesota Vikings, head coach Dan Campbell and quarterback Jared Goff addressed losing linebacker Jack Campbell to injury and broke down how Detroit pulled out the...
articles.body_text:
After the Lions’ gritty win over the Minnesota Vikings, head coach Dan Campbell and quarterback Jared Goff addressed losing linebacker Jack Campbell to injury and broke down how Detroit pulled out the division victory.

The pain of watching Jack Campbell collapse helplessly on the Ford Field turf Sunday has not completely subsided for the Detroit Lions. It certainly is not forgotten by teammates on defense that spent those horrible moments wiping away tears as their captain lay motionless with a neck injury.

But four days later, following Campbell's mostly positive report about having lower body motion, the focus has shifted to how to continue handling the situation.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The prayers persist. That hasn't stopped.

LIONS' JACK CAMPBELL OPENS UP ABOUT NECK INJURY, ANNOUNCES LOWER BODY MOVEMENT BUT ACKNOWLEDGES CHALLENGES

Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard takes notes before a play against Minnesota Vikings during the second half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

But the anguish, despair and despondency are yielding to something different. Something better:

"You're kidding yourself to say it's not hard for the players to see something like that happen to anyone, let alone a player of his stature, of his makeup, of his heart," Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard said on Thursday. "And to think these players are going to walk back in here like nothing happened?

"So the theme has been, let's prepare and play like 46 – every day."

Sheppard said a key fourth-down calls he made toward the end of Sunday's game was calling a blitz against the Minnesota Vikings when that is not typical for the Lions. He said the message to players then was, "we're about to do this for 46," which is Campbell's number.

Trainers tend to Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell after an injury during the fourth quarter against the Minnesota Vikings at Ford Field in Detroit, Mich., on Nov. 1, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

That approach has extended through this week.

"I wake up [thinking] 'what would 46 want me to do today?' Sheppard said. "Would he want us to sulk and feel sorry? I can guarantee you, y'all know Jack, absolutely not. He'd be p---ed off if he found out guys were crying and guys were about him. That's just his makeup.

"So that's what we're doing in everything we do. Every meeting I told the unit, every walkthrough, every play, you all know how Jack prepares. You all know how he plays. The way you honor him is to wipe those tears from your eyes and make sure we prepare and play like him.

"So that's the thing moving forward to this week."

Detroit Lions star Aidan Hutchinson walks near other players as medical staff help linebacker Jack Campbell during the second half of an NFL football game Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya)

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Sheppard cannot deny the emotions his players invested on the scary and uncertain moments while Campbell was being placed on a immobilization board and carted off the field.

But the NFL season has not stopped since the game moved ahead. And like the game, the season continues for the Lions.

And so Sheppard is asking his defensive players to accept something horrible, acknowledge it, and not only overcome it but turn it into a tool.

"That is," Sheppard repeated "the theme for the week."

articles.title: Saudi coalition intercepts missile fired towards Medina
articles.excerpt:
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis has said it intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Iran-aligned armed group towards the Medina region, home to one of Islam’s holiest cities.

Th...
articles.body_text:
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis has said it intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Iran-aligned armed group towards the Medina region, home to one of Islam’s holiest cities.

The announcement on Thursday came just minutes after Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency warned of potential danger in the area near the strategic port of Yanbu.

“Air defence intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the Medina region,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said in a post on X.

The Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have rejected any suggestion they were targeting the city, saying such accusations were a “blatant and grave falsehood”.

Houthi Military spokesman Yahya Saree wrote on X that “our operations target only oil facilities and military bases” and called the allegation a lie.

Among their attacks on airports, energy infrastructure and military sites, the Houthis have targeted the port of Yanbu on several occasions in recent months.

“A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Yanbu Governorate to alert of a potential danger,” read a statement published by the agency online.

The agency later announced that the threat had passed.

Yanbu is a ⁠⁠major oil export hub ⁠⁠and a ⁠⁠key ⁠⁠outlet for oil shipments ‌‌transported through the kingdom’s ‌‌East-West ‌‌pipeline.

The port and pipeline have played a key role since the outbreak of the United States-Israeli war on Iran in February, helping Riyadh ship crude and fuel to global markets.

Separately,  Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces made gains in the Sanamat area in Taiz governorate, where fighting continues to rage.

Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said on Thursday that government forces carried out 1,298 “targeting operations” against the Houthis in the past 24 hours and “managed to gain control” of Sanamat.

The latest operations killed about 400 Houthi fighters and destroyed 132 vehicles, cars or heavy weapons placements, he said. Al Jazeera could not independently verify the claims.

Yemeni government forces previously reclaimed Taiz’s Dhubab district and key positions near the critical Bab al-Mandeb strait.

Meanwhile, on the al-Jawf front, military engineering units continue to clear recaptured sites of mines and booby traps, al-Nazili added.

Late last month, the government said 16,100 Houthi operatives and commanders had been killed or wounded since October 5.

The Houthis have not confirmed a death toll and have in the meantime been firing missiles regularly towards Saudi Arabia, hitting multiple airports and disrupting air traffic over the kingdom.

Yazeed al-Jeddawy, a research manager at the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the course of the conflict increasingly appears to be moving towards a prolonged war of attrition as the government offensive has not shifted the balance of power over the past 30 days.

“The conflict is no longer driven solely by the dynamics inside Yemen; it is intertwined with the wider regional confrontation and the war involving Iran,” he added.

articles.title: Vector introduces ready-to-go one-way attack drone
articles.excerpt:
Utah-based defense company Vector has unveiled the Warfighter’s Stack, an integrated one-way attack drone system that combines its Mace quadcopter, electronic arming device and a controller.

In a Nov...
articles.body_text:
Utah-based defense company Vector has unveiled the Warfighter’s Stack, an integrated one-way attack drone system that combines its Mace quadcopter, electronic arming device and a controller.

In a Nov. 2 announcement, Andy Yakulis, Vector’s co-founder and chief executive officer, said the stack was designed for intuitive operation and scaled production.

“Modern warfare requires more than individual platforms. It requires systems that work together, operators who can employ them effectively, and the industrial capacity to produce them at the scale the mission demands,” Yakulis said.

The Warfighter’s Stack builds on Vector’s experience participating in the Defense Department’s Drone Dominance Program, an effort to rapidly expand and improve the domestic commercial drone industry through competition.

The Pentagon also uses the program to identify top-performing drone manufacturers and place orders with them. Vector ranked fourth in the close-quarters battle category during the latest round of competition, resulting in a government order for 5,000 of its drones.

According to the company, the Warfighter’s Stack consists of the Mace drone, a High-Voltage Electronic Safe and Arm Device, or HV-ESAD, and the Hilt hand controller. “Together, the systems connect the aircraft, energetic integration, and controller into a single operational architecture,” the company said.

Vector described the Mace as a compact, attritable drone — meaning inexpensive and relatively easy to replace — designed to maneuver through “confined and complex environments.”

According to Vector, the drone features low-light and thermal cameras, electronic warfare-resistant capabilities and support for fiber-optic control. It also includes an altitude-hold feature intended to reduce operator workload.

Additionally, the Mace can integrate with the Android Team Awareness Kit, or ATAK, and supports both ArduPilot and Betaflight piloting firmware.

The company’s HV-ESAD is a universal system designed to integrate with a range of drone platforms and munitions. Vector said the modular device was selected to support the Drone Dominance Program.

The company said the Hilt controller was built “around the requirements of the modern warfighter,” with a design intended for use with gloved hands and alongside other military equipment.

Yakulis described the controller as “a purpose-built interface that is rugged, adaptable, and designed to work with the systems they are actually operating.”

According to the announcement, Vector designed the Warfighter’s Stack with production scale in mind and says it can “fulfill orders in the thousands.” However, the company declined to provide details on contracts or timelines.

Daniel Terrill is a contributor to Military Times. He’s been reporting on military issues, the gun industry, and the outdoors for nearly two decades. Although writing is his passion, he’s been a Marine, police officer, and, perhaps the most dangerous job of his career, a substitute teacher.

articles.body_text:
Fox News correspondent Christina Coleman reports on Democratic lawmakers warning Trump administration officials of potential subpoenas and investigations, while party leaders emphasize affordability and downplay impeachment efforts.

FIRST ON FOX: House GOP leadership is giving Republican lawmakers a new playbook to go up against an expected barrage of Democrat-led investigations in the new Congress.

Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., wrote a letter to the current chairs of House committees on Thursday warning them to "maximize our remaining days in power to prepare for what is coming" with instructions on how to brace for those expected probes. A source sent a copy of that letter to Fox News Digital.

"House Democrats have signaled they intend to impeach President Trump, but they will not stop there. They will weaponize every single gavel to appease their radical base," Scalise said. "They will use their oversight authorities to harass the President, his family, cabinet officials, and they will seek to destroy our allies. You all will be a key line of defense in this fight."

The guidance includes three key points: "taking inventory" of current and likely future investigative efforts by Democrats while they are in the minority, identifying who is on Democrats' target list, and reviewing how recent Supreme Court rulings as well as a Department of Justice (DOJ) memo on executive privilege could factor into future investigations.

‘LAWYER UP’: DEMOCRATS, REPUBLICANS WASTE NO TIME IN SETTING SOCIAL MEDIA ABLAZE AFTER MIDTERM SWEEP

President Donald Trump delivers remarks during a campaign rally at the Ocean Center Arena on Oct. 30, 2026, in Daytona Beach, Fla. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Democrats' targets could include "administration officials, programs and authorities, and external allies, including conservative partners and industry leaders," Scalise said.

He added that his staff would meet with the relevant committees and others to further prepare.

"Please let me know if there are any additional tools or support you need from me as you undertake this important effort," Scalise wrote. "I have full confidence that we will be effective in our efforts to fight back as a team."

DEMOCRAT SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN

Democrats have signaled they are poised for a wide range of investigations targeting Trump's Cabinet, family, businesses, and allies as soon as they take over Congress next year.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the likely next head of the House Oversight Committee, released a brief statement Tuesday night when it was projected Democrats would win the House: "Lawyer up."

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, joined by House Majority Whip Tom Emmer and Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, holds a news conference after a House Republican Conference meeting at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 13, 2026. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

DEMOCRAT IMMEDIATELY THREATENS SUBPOENAS FOR TECH EXECUTIVES IN WAKE OF MIDTERMS

The committee said in the statement, "Following this win, Garcia will become Chairman of the House Oversight Committee, where he has vowed to take on the Trump Crime Family, corporate corruption, DHS and ICE abuses, and the cover-up of the Epstein files. His statement can be found below."

House Homeland Security Committee Democrats have similarly signaled they are preparing to probe Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

MIKE JOHNSON NOT RUNNING TO LEAD HOUSE GOP AFTER HISTORIC MIDTERM LOSSES

Meanwhile, a spokeswoman for House Judiciary Committee Democrats told Fox News Digital in response to Scalise's letter, "Sounds like Rep. Scalise is asking his fellow Republicans to compile a list of all the corruption, lawlessness, and abuse they’ve been protecting from congressional oversight. But the people have spoken, and the cover-up expires with the Republican majority. The days of invertebrate congressional submission are over."

The letter comes a day after Scalise launched a bid to become House minority leader in the new Congress.

He will be up against House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, for the job.

Fox News Digital reached out to Democrats on the House Oversight Committee for comment.

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

German Army Chief Christian Freuding will become the country’s chief of defense, assuming the job of Germany’s highest-ranking soldier in February 2027, the defense ministry said in a statement on Thursday.

He will succeed Carsten Breuer, who was chosen as the next head of NATO’s military committee, the alliance’s top military authority and a key advisory body for its political leaders.

Freuding became army chief in October 2025 after years of overseeing Berlin’s arms supplies to Kyiv, pushing for the implementation of new technology tested in Ukraine and initiating a drone regiment in the German army.

“Lieutenant General Freuding embodies camaraderie and the values of our Bundeswehr,” Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said in the statement.

“He is guided by a clear moral compass,” the minister added. “He has impressively demonstrated that, even in times of major changes and challenges, he keeps a cool head, makes the right decisions quickly, and puts them into action.”

Following ...
articles.body_text:
Hundreds of billions of dollars in market value has been wiped from major tech firms in a stock market rout after the US midterm elections sparked concerns of a slowdown in AI development.

Following Democratic wins after election campaigns run on slowing AI, shares in firms across the tech and artificial intelligence sectors plummeted.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite stock index closed down by more than 5.5% to lose an estimated $2.5tn in market capitalisation, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses in their worst days since 2025.

The sell-off comes on top of broader concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.

Democrats in races across the US  campaigned to slow the onslaught of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology.

Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.

Shares in companies heavily exposed to AI data centres, including crucial chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers, fell sharply on Thursday, highlighting investor concerns that had already been growing.

Nvidia shares slid more than 9%, knocking more than $400bn off the firm's market value.

Other chipmakers also suffered, with AMD and Micron both dropping by more than 17%. Intel shares also dropped, down 10.3%, while memory card maker SanDisk plunged more than 22%.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks the performance of 30 of the largest companies involved in semiconductor production, fell by more than 12%.

Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value on Thursday.

Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night.

In total, the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, have shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day.

The stock falls also hit other major US stock indexes. The S&P 500 index fell by 4.4% by the end of trading, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased gains made on Wednesday to close down more than 3.4%.

The Nasdaq Composite fall was so large it is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high.

Live: What can Democrats do with control of Congress? We answer your US midterms questions

Food, fuel and taxes – can the Democrats actually make life cheaper?

Boebert, billionaires' tax and other midterms races still to watch

Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets.

"Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said.

"Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction."

Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.

OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board.

"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening.

Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick said that the industry needed to put more effort into selling AI as a good idea.

"I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference.

Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction.

articles.title: Delhi's toxic winter air is back - is the Indian capital prepared for pollution?
articles.excerpt:
People exercise in a park in Delhi on Thursday, breathing in hazy, polluted air

There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling...
articles.body_text:
People exercise in a park in Delhi on Thursday, breathing in hazy, polluted air

There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers.

"The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher.

She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air.

Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. But as winter sets in, the air often becomes unbearable.

Falling temperatures and slower winds trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. Smoke from crop residue burning in neighbouring states adds to emissions from vehicles and factories, as well as construction dust. Firecrackers used during festivals often worsen air quality.

The result is noxious air and a familiar question: why does pollution return year after year, and why hasn't more been done to tackle it?

This year, however, the Delhi government announced its Winter Action Plan months before the worst of the smog arrived. The plan is in place from 1 November to 28 February, covering the months when pollution usually spikes.

Experts have called this a step in the right direction, noting that in previous years measures were often rolled out only after the air quality got too bad to ignore. However, they say this by itself won't be enough, calling for more holistic, long-lasting measures.

Just days after the plan came into effect, the city is slipping back into a depressingly familiar pattern.

This week, a grey haze hangs over Delhi, along with a distinct smoky smell that residents unwillingly recognise. People complain of irritation in their eyes and difficulty breathing, and coughs and sneezes are heard everywhere.

For those who can afford them, air purifiers have become a household necessity. Outdoors, people wear masks or cover their faces with cloth, trying to protect themselves from the worst of the pollution.

Anti-smog guns sprinkle water to settle atmospheric dust in Delhi

Tackling pollution was among the promises made by the governing Bharatiya Janata Party during its election campaign last year. Its winter action plan is now a major test of that pledge.

The plan restricts the entry of older, more polluting vehicles registered outside Delhi and denies fuel to vehicles without a certificate which shows they meet emission standards. Demolitions and outdoor construction work that generate dust have been temporarily banned.

Private vehicle use is being discouraged - the government has asked offices to allow half of their employees to work from home, introduced staggered office timings for its staff and doubled parking charges. It says it will also strengthen pollution monitoring and enforcement and promote public transport and electric vehicles.

These measures are separate from the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap), which is overseen by the federal Commission for Air Quality Management.

Grap introduces restrictions in stages, with stricter measures kicking in as pollution levels rise. This week, its second stage is in force, restricting the use of diesel generators and burning of coal and firewood.

Expert say on paper, these actions collectively provide a roadmap for responding to rising pollution levels but their success ultimately depends on enforcement.

"There are a lot of positive changes as far as planning is concerned, but when it comes to execution, we probably still stand at the same level," says Parthaa Bosu, strategic adviser at the Environmental Defense Fund, a non-profit group focused on delivering climate solutions.

Others argue that the problem goes much deeper.

Vehicle entry restrictions have led to huge jams at Delhi's borders

"If we want to reduce pollution, we need to set targets for every sector - including power generation, industry and transport - not just vehicle entry, construction and stubble burning," says Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

"We know how much each sector and each state contributes to pollution. We can set targets to reduce emissions from each of them over the next five years."

Bosu points out that an issue which does not get enough attention is secondary pollutants - when gases in the air react with sunlight, water vapour and other substances to form harmful particles that contribute to pollution.

"Pollution is not just caused by biomass burning or vehicles," he says. "Dust being stirred up from the ground, coal and fly ash, materials burned at brick kilns and the large-scale burning of urban waste are also contributing to the problem. And much of this is still not being stopped."

Delhi's pollution problem is also affected by what happens outside the city. Pollutants travel into Delhi from neighbouring states and other parts of northern India, worsening the situation, Bosu explains.

This means that measures taken by Delhi can achieve only so much. Tackling the problem requires neighbouring states and the wider northern region to work together, he adds.

'I panic every time she coughs' - Delhi's toxic air is making its children sick

Why India caps pollution reading at 500 when the air is far more toxic

Can artificial rain fix toxic air in India's capital?

Living in Delhi smog is like watching a dystopian film again and again

In the meantime, pollution is harming people's health every day.

During winter, government monitoring stations in Delhi frequently record Air Quality Index (AQI) readings above 300, classified as "very poor".

On particularly bad days, readings can reach 500, the highest point on India's scale. That does not mean pollution cannot rise further, only that domestic trackers do not record it. International trackers such as Swiss-based IQAir have recorded readings close to 1,000 on some days.

The World Health Organization recommends average PM2.5 levels over 24 hours should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic metre. In Delhi, levels are often at more than 25 times that limit during pollution season.

Dr Manoj Goel, pulmonology unit head at Fortis Memorial Research Institute near Delhi, says these tiny particles "can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, triggering inflammation and affecting multiple organs".

Even short-term exposure can cause throat irritation, coughing, wheezing and breathlessness. It can also worsen existing heart and lung conditions.

A 2025 report, external by the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago estimated that air pollution could reduce life expectancy in Delhi by up to 8.2 years.

Burning of crop residue in neighbouring states is among the contributors to Delhi's pollution

For residents, the challenge is not just limited to breathing. The restrictions also disrupt everyday life.

Delhi is closely connected to its satellite towns, Noida and Gurugram, with thousands of people travelling between them every day for work. Long queues form at the city's borders as vehicles are stopped and checked, leaving commuters stuck in traffic for hours.

While the new rules offer some hope, frustration is growing.

Protests, political arguments and court interventions have become part of the annual cycle. But despite public pressure and government measures, the pollution returns every winter.

Rana keeps her windows closed and curtains drawn, and has added more indoor plants.

The arrival of another winter fills her family with dread, but unlike many others, they are not planning to move out of Delhi.

"I would have left the city long ago had there been an option, but my son has his school, my husband and I have our jobs as well, which makes it practically impossible," she says.

"What option do we have? It is unfair but we will have to live with it."

articles.title: California governor commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates
articles.excerpt:
California Governor Gavin Newsom's term in office comes to an end in January

California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing th...
articles.body_text:
California Governor Gavin Newsom's term in office comes to an end in January

California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison.

"We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.

The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.

The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.

Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday.

Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole.

"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".

California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.

Americans' views on death penalty after failed execution in Tennessee

Describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", Newsom said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".

He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.

Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.

He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me".

"As governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote.

"For this reason, I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."

Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.

Bernard E Harcourt, a law and civil liberties professor at Columbia University, told the BBC that it is not unprecedented for a potential presidential candidate to come out as an abolitionist in the run up to elections - despite the overall popularity of the death penalty in the US.

He noted that François Mitterrand did precisely that in his presidential campaign in France in 1981, taking "the higher ethical ground and was rewarded by the public for that".

"I detect a very similar ethical positioning in Governor Newsom's statements about the commutations. And here too, it may well be something that the voters respect," he said.

San Quentin State Prison's used to house California's death row adjustment centre

Newsom's decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.

At least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court will have to sign off on the commutations, CalMatters reported.

It is unclear how Newsom's decision will affect condemned inmates like Keith Doolin, 53, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for murdering two sex workers, Inez Espinoza and Peggy Tucker, and shooting four others. He maintains his innocence.

Doolin lived on death row at San Quentin for decades, until he was moved to another prison in 2025 when the governor announced the state would reform the prison for all but those on death row.

Doolin's mother, Donna Larsen, told the BBC that the news of Newsom's commutations - which includes Doolin - brought mixed emotions.

"At least the execution chamber will not be reconstructed, and no more killing by the people of the state of California," she said.

Anthony D Romero, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, applauded Newsom's action.

"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," Romero said.

"By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialised injustice head-on."

Nathan Hochman, the top prosecutor in Los Angeles County, said that while Newsom has the power to commute sentences, only state legislature or voters can eliminate the death penalty.

"Californians have been asked on two separate ballot initiatives to abolish the death penalty and both times they have chosen to keep it for the most serious crimes," Hochman said in a statement.

How widely used is the death penalty in the US?

On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".

In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.

While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty.

No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.

The death penalty is legal in 27 states, but has been abolished in 23 states and Washington DC, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a national non-profit.

California, which primarily uses lethal injection for executions, used to house male death row prisoners in San Quentin State Prison north of San Francisco, and female inmates in the Central California Women's Facility in the Central Valley.

But a 2016 ballot measure allowed for their transfer to other facilities that provide a necessary level of security, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.

Why the death penalty is on the rise in US

US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution

articles.title: Powerhouse Parramatta opens this weekend – and it’s dazzling inside and out
articles.excerpt:
Coups de théâtre abound in the $915m addition to western Sydney’s skyline, which opens on Saturday with five new exhibitions – and a 23-day festival

Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email

Dubbe...
articles.body_text:
Coups de théâtre abound in the $915m addition to western Sydney’s skyline, which opens on Saturday with five new exhibitions – and a 23-day festival

Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email

Dubbed the “Opera House of western Sydney”, Powerhouse Parramatta’s white lattice exoskeleton, composed from 1,300 individual pieces and wrapping 30,000 sq metres of interior space, has already become a familiar landmark.

Even better known, perhaps, is the project’s controversial history. Since the Parramatta outpost was announced in 2014, a vocal group of dissenters led by former staff and trustees has lamented what they see as the neglect of the museum’s Ultimo site in favour of a new infrastructure project, and what they say is a shift away from the museum’s core business towards contemporary art and events.

The eye-watering price tag – $915m, in an era of funding precarity for the arts – has also come under scrutiny, culminating in a New South Wales Treasury investigation into allegations over the museum’s governance and procurement practices. In late August, 10 weeks from the scheduled opening, CEO Lisa Havilah was stood down while the investigation unfolded.

When the major new venue opens to the public on Saturday, the big question will be: was it worth it? What will it bring to Parramatta – and will it be enough to bring the rest of Sydney, and the rest of Australia, out west?

Powerhouse is sweetening the pot with a 23-day opening festival of performances, parties, talks, screenings and workshops, with 65% of the program free. When Guardian Australia visited last week, the space was crowded with installation crew in hi-vis, hard hats and steel-capped boots. But even with its exhibitions in various states of readiness, it was hard not to be dazzled.

The steel exoskeleton that has been such a prominent addition to Parramatta’s skyline is more than decorative. Encasing two towers, and built from 12,000 tonnes of steel, it’s what allows the building to boast massive column-free exhibition spaces up to 18m in height, including the largest in Australia.

But at first encounter, perhaps the most striking thing about the Moreau Kusunoki and Genton-designed building is the sense of calm it evokes. This is a building that is constantly calling you to slow down, take a breath and look beyond its architecture to the city, landscape and Parramatta River below.

The glass facade and abundance of natural light is complemented by an airy colour palette, all creams, white and light greys – including interior walls covered in a pale, textured render made from 600,000 crushed oyster shells, locally and sustainably sourced. Wide corridors flanking the exhibition spaces are lined with chairs and lounges that invite you to pause and take in the view.

This peace is particularly necessary given the dizzying spectacles of Powerhouse Parramatta’s five opening exhibitions – including a tribute to space and flight; a celebration of the shopping mall; a kids’ exhibition themed around the dark; and a showcase of British designer Es Devlin – which otherwise risk sensory overload.

Sign up for the fun stuff with our rundown of must-reads, pop culture and tips for the weekend, every Sunday morning

Coups de théâtre abound: secret doorways and dramatic reveals; a mirror maze; a copse of Christmas firs; a massive replica meteorite taking up an entire exhibition space. There’s a recreation of the historic Roselands shopping mall fountain; a restored 1920s elevator transporting visitors with access needs between exhibition floors; and a rainbow-hued walk-in installation by American light artist James Turrell at the top of a tower.

Throughout the spaces, museum objects (more than 1,600 from the 500,000-strong collection, supplemented by around as many loans) jostle with specially commissioned artworks, lavishly designed displays and interactive exhibits. The exhibitions are fuelled by wonder, spectacle and nostalgia – and are hard to resist.

Task Eternal is Powerhouse Parramatta’s flagship opening exhibition – and the only one that adults will have to pay an entry fee for ($30/$20 concession; 16 and unders get in free). A celebration of flight and space travel, it takes over the museum’s main hall: 2,000 sq metres with 18-metre-high ceilings, bringing together objects from the Powerhouse collection as well as loans, commissions and literary texts – including excerpts from US science fiction author Ted Chiang, whose short story Tower of Babylon inspired the exhibition’s structure, including a zigzagging tower which visitors ascend and descend.

Hero items include delicate sketches by Leonardo da Vinci; a bumarang (boomerang) – an example of ingenious Indigenous aerodynamic design – collected from Burramatta/Parramatta in the early 19th century; a “boilerplate” (or testing model) Apollo command module from the 1960s; and the spacesuit worn by Leonard Nimoy’s Spock in Star Trek.

Aircraft from different eras, including the ingenious 19th-century flying rigs of Australian aviation pioneer Lawrence Hargrave, take pride of place. There is an entire room full of engines, and lots of rockets too, including a Skylark research rocket deployed at Woomera in the 70s, and a fully functional retro Rocket Playground from the 1960s.

Among the many stunning artworks, the star exhibit – at the top of the tower – is a perception-testing “ganzfeld” installation by US light artist James Turrell, accessible for those who bought a special Turrell-inclusive ticket ($40 for adults, $10 for kids). Eight viewers at a time are invited into a room with curved walls and a shifting cycle of coloured light, which induces the kind of disorientation experienced by pilots in certain altitudes and atmospheres.

Task Eternal is overwhelming in its scope and visual magnificence. It’s also a little discombobulating. Rather than chronology, it is structured around four “acts” exploring not only the history and technology of air and space travel, but our “cultural relationship with the sky” and “the human compulsion to ascend, leave Earth and return”. It zigzags between eras, topics and modes of storytelling; between science, engineering, design and art.

It also works hard to shed the western, patriarchal and colonial narratives around space and flight, and to weave in lesser-known histories and perspectives, including First Nations technologies and cosmologies. This doesn’t make for a smooth, coherent journey; though time, attention to wall texts and repeat visits may yield the kind of rich experience it aims for.

The Mall, a tribute to the social, cultural and design history of shopping centres, was only partially installed a week ahead of opening, but looks to be similarly maximalist. The Dark, the Powerhouse’s exhibition for children aged 4 to 12 set in a massive replica meteorite more than 22m long, will be an absolute hit – and not just because it’s top secret: no photographs are allowed, and visitors will have to bag their smartphones before entering.

We are allowed to describe how it works though: visitors enter via a dark, narrow tunnel followed by a series of glowing chambers, lined and stuffed with more than 800 objects, including sparkling minerals, retro toys, ancient artefacts and modern treasures (including the first item the museum collected, in 1882: a jar of peas). Part playground, part discovery trail, items are arranged from toddler to adult height, and there are enough hidden delights and nostalgic treats to thaw the most frosty heart – including animations drawing on First Nations creation stories, and the museum’s most Googled object: a heart-emblazoned shirt worn by Leonardo DiCaprio in Baz Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet. There’s not much narrative here, and some might grumble that it is light on science and learning, but museums desperately need to attract young audiences – and this might do the trick.

The calmest of the opening exhibits, titled Overflow, is an installation on the eastern building’s third floor: a 16-metre high-definition LED display of short films by director Ivan Sen, featuring breathtaking footage, each spotlighting one of seven Indigenous organisations from NSW who care for water, country and community.

In front of the screen is a shallow pool with water that laps with the tides of the river. Visitors are encouraged to take their shoes off and get their feet wet; there’s a sensorial magic about being 30m high, with your feet in the water and the sky on either side of you.

“We’re on a flood plain,” says Beau James, director of First Nations for the Powerhouse, gesturing to the Parramatta River out the window. In fact the location of the building was its own controversy for that very reason. “That river has always ebbed and flowed, that’s its natural way of moving. We wanted to honour water.”

As part of the commission, the museum invested an undisclosed amount of money in the organisations featured in Sen’s films. “We asked them: ‘What’s something you’ve always really wanted to do but have never been able to get funds for?’” says James.

The funded proposals include tagging marine life in Gamay (Botany Bay); clearing rubbish and mitigating pollution in the Parramatta River; and an initiative for clearing invasive European carp from the Barwon River in Brewarrina.

The final exhibition brings together recent works by British designer Es Devlin whose peripatetic career has encompassed theatre, fashion, public art and arena concerts (she has designed tours for Beyoncé, U2 and Lady Gaga, as well as Olympic ceremonies and Super Bowl half-time shows).

But Powerhouse’s exhibition – her Australian debut – sees Devlin in a more poetic and philosophical mode. Made over the last decade (and adjusted here for their Australian debuts), the five works, spread across four main rooms, represent Devlin’s attempts to use participatory art and interactive design to induce shifts of awareness and perspective; and to help rewire our sense of connection to the living world and each other.

The visual highlight is a giant mirror maze, designed to represent the “arterial geometries of lungs and trees”. But the soul of the exhibition is the participatory work Collective Portrait: a room with a 24m table and an equally long, unspooling reel of white paper, with an invitation to sit down on either side of the table for 15 minutes and draw the person opposite you.

The point is not so much the drawing as the silent interpersonal exchange between strangers. “I’ve been practising this around the world, and I’ve found whoever I practise it with, it can be quietly transformational,” says Devlin.

She has also created a sixth, temporary work for the museum’s month-long opening festival: an Australian iteration of her 2022 outdoor work Come Home Again, featuring her own hand-drawn sketches of 244 endangered local species, and choral tributes which will be performed at dusk most nights through November within her illuminated outdoor installation on the Powerhouse’s riverside lawn.

“I’m hoping that if we set up the rhythm of these evensong moments over the opening days and weeks, that people will continue to gather here. That it’s like a beacon.”

Devlin, who has exhibited in the world’s top galleries and museums, describes Powerhouse Parramatta as a “magnificent” building with “astounding” opening exhibitions. “The fact that people are going to not just learn things but feel things and therefore remember what they learned? I think it’s going to make it a destination for people to come from far and wide.”

articles.title: MLW's Trevor Lee set for major high-stakes match against Yota Tsuji at Saturday Night SuperFight

Trevor Lee sets his sights on his biggest opportunity yet: IWGP heavyweight champion Yota Tsuji.

Trevor Lee officially signed with Major League Wrestling (MLW) seven months ago and he has kept his fo...
articles.body_text:
Trevor Lee sets his sights on his biggest opportunity yet: IWGP heavyweight champion Yota Tsuji.

Trevor Lee officially signed with Major League Wrestling (MLW) seven months ago and he has kept his foot on the gas pedal since stepping in between the ropes for the company.

Lee has gone toe-to-toe with some of the best MLW has to offer, including Kushida, Austin Aries and Místico, while also holding the MLW Southern Crown Championship. He broke the news with OutKick Dropkick/Fox News Digital in April and said at the time he had been waiting for a good opportunity to come his way.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Trevor Lee gets the crowd riled up during a Major League Wrestling show. (Major League Wrestling)

Lee will have a chance to make a statement at Saturday Night SuperFight this weekend when he steps into the ring with IWGP heavyweight champion Yota Tsuji, who is a superstar with New Japan Pro-Wrestling.

"I think it’s been going great," Lee told OutKick Dropkick of his time with MLW so far. "I think with the last time we spoke, I probably said something along the lines of, I just want to go out there and show what I can do, and I feel like over these past few months, I've had the capability to do that. I think that we're gonna be looking at even more opportunity coming this Saturday when I wrestle Yota. I mean, I couldn't ask for a better opportunity, right? The IWGP heavyweight champion. I'm looking at this match like kind of like a job interview, right? And, what a way to, what a way to try to start it out."

Lee was the one who called out Tsuji for this match at one of MLW’s biggest shows of the year.

MLW'S COURT BAUER TOUTS 'HUGE YEAR' FOR COMPANY AMID MEDIA DEALS, SPLASH MOVES

Yota Tsuji will take on Trevor Lee on Nov. 7, 2026. (MLW)

Tsuji is a two-time IWGP heavyweight champion, two-time IWGP global heavyweight champion and has held the IWGP Intercontinental Championship and the NEVER Openweight 6-Man Tag Team Championship one-time each.

The stakes are as high as they could be going into this match.

"I wanna show that I'm ready for that opportunity and if we're gonna bring these guys in and we're gonna highlight these guys as being the top guys that they truly are, Yota is the top of the top at New Japan," he continued. "So, if he's gonna come over here and he's gonna ask for a fight, then, you know, I'm looking for an opportunity. And I told you that right the last time we spoke, that I'm just wanting opportunities and what bigger opportunity."

Tsuji already has a cast of wrestlers gunning for his title. Most recently, it was Boltin Oleg and Kenny Omega.

Though Saturday night’s match is a non-title fight, the potential of Lee pinning Tsuji may put him among the contenders for the IWGP Heavyweight Championship.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

OutKick Dropkick asked Lee if he’s thought about that possibility.

"One-hundred percent," he said. "I'd love to wrestle for New Japan. I've never wrestled for New Japan. I've wrestled for a lot of companies in, in my career, but, I've never had the opportunity to even go to Japan and wrestle in Japan. So, what better way to step in day one to show everybody, hey, I've already beat the top guy here and, and I'm ready to continue to do it again."

Lee vs. Tsuji is one of seven matches on the massive Saturday Night SuperFight card, which will feature MLW world heavyweight champion Killer Kross going up against Josh Bishop in a last man standing match for the title.

Major League Wrestling's Trevor Lee seen in action during a show. (Major League Wrestling)

Lee predicted that the Chicago crowd will be "rocking" as MLW brings a different style of pro wrestling to the masses.

articles.title: Bill Belichick advances once again as Pro Football Hall of Fame finalist after first-ballot snub in 2026
articles.excerpt: Brian Urlacher criticizes NFL Hall of Fame voters for denying Bill Belichick first-ballot status, arguing that the decision sets a precedent that there may never be a first-ballot coach in the Hall of...
articles.body_text:
Brian Urlacher criticizes NFL Hall of Fame voters for denying Bill Belichick first-ballot status, arguing that the decision sets a precedent that there may never be a first-ballot coach in the Hall of Fame.

Bill Belichick is back where he was last year, as he was among the five coaches that advanced in the process to potentially be elected into the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

No one expected Belichick to still be on the ballot at this point, though, believing he deserved to be a first-ballot Hall of Famer. After all, he has the second-most wins by a head coach of all time, and some believe he is the greatest coach to ever grace an NFL sideline.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

But, despite his many accolades and reverence in the sport, Belichick didn’t make the cut on his first ballot, sending the football world into massive debate and many of his former players speaking out in disgust. Belichick himself was "puzzled" and "disappointed" he wasn’t a first-ballot Hall of Famer, per ESPN.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

New England Patriots head coach Bill Belichick pre-game against the Jets at MetLife Stadium on Oct. 21, 2019. (Robert Deutsch/USA TODAY Sports)

One year later, Belichick could, and should, be in the Hall of Fame Class of 2027, as the governing body announced that next step for him and four other coaches on Thursday.

Joining Belichick are great former coaches Tom Coughlin, Dan Reeves, Mike Holmgren and Mike Shanahan from the group of 14 who were considered. The coaching subcommittee will meet next on Nov. 17 to pick one from the final five to be presented in front of the voting committee for the 2027 class.

Belichick moved on in 2026, and it’s highly expected he will do so again. So, the question becomes: will he now get at least the 40 votes needed to be placed in Canton for eternity?

This is a head coach who tallied six Super Bowls with the New England Patriots, while owning two prior to that with the New York Giants as their defensive coordinator. There’s no question his resume speaks for itself, and he even told an associate, per ESPN, "Six Super Bowls isn’t enough?"

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Head coach Bill Belichick of the North Carolina Tar Heels looks on during the second half of a game at Kenan Stadium on Sept. 1, 2025, in Chapel Hill, North Carolina. (Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images)

After Belichick was snubbed, the Hall of Fame overhauled its selection process, cutting the voting committee down from 50 to 28, while ending formal presentations and merging the senior category with modern era.

The Hall says the changes are intended to "improve its selection process."

"The Hall continually reviews its bylaws to ensure the selection process reflects the highest standards of integrity and the magnitude of election to the Pro Football Hall of Fame," said Hall of Fame president Jim Porter in September. "There is no more important task at the Hall of Fame than the election of each new class."

New England Patriots head coach Bill Belichick on the sidelines in 2023. (Robert Deutsch / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)

Belichick is currently in his second season as the head coach of the North Carolina Tar Heels, who sit 4-4 on the year.

articles.title: Sylvester Stallone says Hollywood abandoned Middle America as Taylor Sheridan found an ignored audience
articles.excerpt:
Actor Sylvester Stallone discusses his time working as a movie theater usher on ‘Special Report.’

Sylvester Stallone didn't hold back when it came to Hollywood's biggest blind spot.

The "Tulsa King"...
articles.body_text:
Actor Sylvester Stallone discusses his time working as a movie theater usher on ‘Special Report.’

Sylvester Stallone didn't hold back when it came to Hollywood's biggest blind spot.

The "Tulsa King" star explained Taylor Sheridan found success by giving a forgotten audience exactly what it had been missing. According to Stallone, Sheridan tapped into something Hollywood had long ignored: an audience eager for stories rooted in Middle America.

"It's very, very important because that audience was ignored for centuries, it seems, since John Wayne," Stallone explained during an appearance on "The Rest Is Entertainment." "And he really mined a consciousness like, 'Oh, we forgot about that guy in the middle of America.' They're always writing about California and New York."

TAYLOR SHERIDAN SAYS HOLLYWOOD DIDN’T BELIEVE IN 'YELLOWSTONE,' NOW IT’S A TV EMPIRE

Sylvester Stallone said Hollywood ignored Middle America for generations, dating the trend back to John Wayne. (Steve Swisher/Paramount+)

"But the middle America, it's a different vibe," he added. "And so people were starving for it. It's like a simpler world and more, I would just say, confrontational."

Despite Sheridan's success, Stallone doesn't think Hollywood has caught up when it comes to film-making and what Middle America might be hoping to see on the big screen.

"But the beauty of streaming is they're fast, and they're nimble, and they can really put a show on the air in a matter of weeks," Stallone said.

"Tulsa King" star Sylvester Stallone credited Taylor Sheridan with reaching viewers hungry for stories rooted in Middle America. (Steve Swisher/Paramount+)

articles.title: Firefighter who battled COVID on front lines says he lost career for refusing vaccine: 'I'm on team Jesus'
articles.excerpt: Former Redmond fire Lt. Scott Carlson describes the emotional toll of losing his job after seeking a religious exemption from a COVID-19 vaccine mandate and explains why he continues fighting years la...
articles.body_text:
Former Redmond fire Lt. Scott Carlson describes the emotional toll of losing his job after seeking a religious exemption from a COVID-19 vaccine mandate and explains why he continues fighting years later.

A veteran Washington state firefighter who helped respond to some of America's first COVID-19 patients says he lost the career he loved after refusing to violate his religious beliefs to comply with a vaccine mandate and is now fighting to have his day in court.

Scott Carlson, a former lieutenant with the Redmond Fire Department, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview that he and his colleagues spent 18 months on the front lines of the pandemic without a single case of cross-contamination before the city's vaccine requirements upended his career.

"We worked 18 months with zero cross-contaminations," Carlson said. "We did our job very well. And then the governor came out and said that they wanted us to get the COVID vaccine mandate."

WHO IS JAMES ERDMAN III? CIA WHISTLEBLOWER WHO WENT FROM COVID MANDATE FIGHTS TO SENATE SPOTLIGHT

Scott Carlson, a former lieutenant with the Redmond Fire Department, sits in a fire truck. (First Liberty Institute)

But when Washington officials implemented COVID-19 vaccination requirements, Carlson said he sought a religious exemption in 2021, only to learn that he would not be permitted to continue working. First Liberty Institute, which is representing eight firefighters, did not elaborate on Carlson's behalf regarding his religious exemption request.

"I went through and applied for a religious exemption," Carlson recalled. "I had to prove that I was actually religious, and it wasn't just something I wanted.

"And then, about 10 days later, the mayor [Angela Birney] came back and got rid of all of that and said no, and then decided to terminate all of us."

According to court documents, Carlson filed a lawsuit against the City of Redmond in federal court Dec. 8, 2022, alleging that officials violated Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 by failing to accommodate his religious beliefs and retaliating against him for requesting an exemption from the COVID-19 vaccine mandate.

The lawsuit was later amended twice to include additional firefighters after they received notices from the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission granting them the right to sue, according to the court filing.

The firefighters are appealing a December 2025 federal district court ruling that sided with the City of Redmond, rejecting their claims that the city failed to accommodate their religious beliefs and retaliated against them for seeking exemptions from its COVID-19 vaccine mandate.

Their attorney, Cliff Martin, told Fox News Digital in an interview Wednesday that the case involves more than a disagreement over vaccine policy. He alleges the city had positions available that could have accommodated the firefighters but appeared to keep those opportunities from them.

OREGON SETTLES WITH CHRISTIAN MOTHER DENIED FOSTER CARE ADOPTION OVER GENDER IDENTITY BELIEFS

Scott Carlson, a former lieutenant with the Redmond Fire Department, with his family. (First Liberty Institute)

According to First Liberty, Carlson initially received religious exemptions before those accommodations were revoked after Redmond's mayor signed an executive order. The firefighters' attorneys allege that city officials subsequently withheld information about available positions that could have allowed the employees to remain on the job.

The legal team is asking the 9th Circuit to overturn a lower court ruling that rejected their claims.

"We're at the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, and we are hopeful that the circuit court will reverse a summary judgment order and will recognize and vindicate the victims of this religious discrimination," Martin told Fox News Digital.

Martin alleged that the employer could have transferred the firefighters into other roles where vaccination was not required.

"Instead, they hid those available positions from the plaintiffs and then filled them with vaccinated firefighters so that there was nowhere to transfer these unvaccinated firefighters who had a religious objection to the COVID vaccine," he said.

WASHINGTON SCHOOL DISTRICT THAT FORCED KIDS TO HIDE BIBLES IN SEALED ENVELOPES MUST APOLOGIZE, PAY $275K

Scott Carlson, a former lieutenant with the Redmond Fire Department, stands by an American flag. (First Liberty Institute)

Those allegations are central to the firefighters' legal challenge and have not been independently established in the interview material provided to Fox News Digital.

For Carlson, the consequences went far beyond losing a paycheck.

He said firefighting was a calling that allowed him to serve his community, use his skills and help others during some of the most difficult moments of their lives.

"The emotion of losing my career, and what I feel a little bit is what my purpose is, over my faith, that was a heart divided, because I love Jesus so much that I was like, ‘Hey, I'm going to follow you no matter what. I'm on team Jesus. But dang it, this is hard.’"

Carlson said the loss of his position meant losing an important part of how he served others.

"This is how I serve. This is how I love on the community," he said. "So, that was a very hard emotion to say that I'm no longer going to be able to do this."

Although the COVID-19 pandemic has faded from daily headlines, Carlson said the legal and personal consequences remain unresolved for people who lost their jobs during the vaccine mandate era.

TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS

Scott Carlson, a former lieutenant with the Redmond Fire Department, told Fox News Digital employees should never have to choose between their faith and their job. (First Liberty Institute)

"A lot of people say, ‘Oh, COVID's over, the pandemic's over,’ and a lot of people have varying opinions about it," Carlson said. "Most of those opinions have changed. Most people are shocked to hear that things aren't done. They hear, ‘Oh, hey, the military is having some of these cases or some of these things changed,’ or somebody else has had a success or a victory in this sense."

Martin said the appeal raises fundamental questions about the extent of employers' obligations to consider religious accommodations.

"No employee should have to choose between their faith and their job here," Martin said.

A spokesperson for the City of Redmond told Fox News Digital that the city "does not comment on pending or ongoing litigation. The City will continue to address this matter through the appropriate legal channels."

A spokesperson for the Redmond mayor's office told Fox News Digital it could only refer to the city's statement due to the ongoing nature of the litigation.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Redmond Fire Department for comment.

Rachel del Guidice is a culture reporter for Fox News covering the intersection of politics, faith, family, and American culture.

articles.title: Generation Z and young voters help redefine US politics after midterms
articles.excerpt:
The outcome of the 2026 US midterm elections has marked a historic shift in American politics, with diverse candidates and the first Gen Z woman to be elected to Congress.

Of the 117 Generation Z can...
articles.body_text:
The outcome of the 2026 US midterm elections has marked a historic shift in American politics, with diverse candidates and the first Gen Z woman to be elected to Congress.

Of the 117 Generation Z candidates who ran for Congress this year, 24 won their primaries and made it to Tuesday’s ballot, according to the organization Future Caucus.

Among them was Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old Ethiopian-born democratic socialist from Colorado, who became the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress.

Kiros, a lawyer turned doctoral student, won a stunning primary victory, the first-time candidate beating 30-year incumbent Representative Diana DeGette in the Denver-area seat.

After she won her primary earlier this year, she told supporters that she was taking the fight to “Donald Trump and the oligarchy”, abolishing US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), passing Medicare for All and ending the “genocide in Palestine”.

She joins Representative Maxwell Frost of Florida, who became the first Gen Z member of the House in 2022.

Young people voted overwhelmingly for Democrats, according to an Associated Press news agency voter poll.

After relatively high support for Trump in the 2024 election, young voters snapped back toward the Democratic Party in this year’s midterms.

The AP Voter Poll showed about 7 in 10 voters under 30 nationally said they supported the Democratic candidate in their local US House race, while about 3 in 10 said they voted for the Republican. That was a dramatic shift from 2024, when the youngest voters were roughly split between Trump and Harris.

Most first-time midterm voters, who skew younger, also mostly supported the Democratic candidate.

Both young voters and first-time voters made up a fairly small share of voters. Only about 1 in 10 voters in the 2026 national electorate are under 30, for instance, which limited the impact of the shift.

But young voters’ displeasure with the country and its leadership was clear. About half of young voters said they were “angry” about the way things were going in the country today, compared with only about one-third of voters ages 65 and older. And about 6 in 10 voters under 30 said one reason for their vote for the US House was to express opposition to Trump, compared to about half of voters ages 30-44, and about 4 in 10 voters ages 45 and older.

Young voters shifted toward the Democrats in each of the Senate races where the Democratic Party picked up a seat, including in Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, and North Carolina.

articles.title: South Africa’s ANC on track for new lows in local polls
articles.excerpt: South Africa’s early municipal election results have shown the African National Congress (ANC) with a sharply reduced vote share, weakening the long-dominant party’s control of key cities such as Joha...
articles.body_text:
South Africa’s early municipal election results have shown the African National Congress (ANC) with a sharply reduced vote share, weakening the long-dominant party’s control of key cities such as Johannesburg.

The ANC was on about 32 percent of the vote, with the Democratic Alliance (DA) in second place at 25 percent, after more than 60 percent of the votes had been counted in this week’s municipal elections, data from the election commission showed late on Thursday.

Meanwhile, former President Jacob Zuma’s breakaway opposition uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party was in third place with 8.5 percent, below levels suggested by opinion polls.

About 15.9 million of 29.2 million registered voters cast ballots, the electoral commission said, putting turnout at an estimated 54.5 percent, up from 46 percent in the pandemic-hit 2021 local elections.

The ANC, which has been South Africa’s largest party since it led the country out of apartheid in 1994, has tended to do worse in municipal elections than nationally and has acknowledged its failures in local governance.

From nearly 70 percent of the national vote in 2004, the ANC fell below 50 percent for the first time in the 2021 municipal elections, winning 46 percent.

At the 2024 national elections, it managed just more than 40 percent and was forced to accept a unity government with nine other parties, including the DA.

The party, now led by President Cyril Ramaphosa, has borne the brunt of criticism about years of municipal mismanagement that have left South Africans grappling with failing water supplies, persistent power cuts and crumbling public services.

It has also faced corruption allegations, while splinter parties have eaten away at its support base.

The results of this week’s local ballot will offer a key measure of voters’ sentiment ahead of the 2029 general election.

Control of the country’s eight major metropolitan municipalities is up for grabs, alongside dozens of district and local councils.

The MK party had been tipped as one of the few parties capable of securing an outright majority in the eastern port city of Durban.

But projections by the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a state-funded research body, put its support there at 32 percent.

The DA, meanwhile, was forecast to retain control of tourist magnet Cape Town with 56 percent of the vote, with its leader, Geordin Hill-Lewis, already declaring victory.

The party was also leading with 34 percent in Johannesburg, the country’s financial capital, after running a spirited campaign spearheaded by its former leader, Helen Zille, 75, according to CSIR projections.

With outright majorities far from assured in several major cities, the results could usher in another round of complex coalition negotiations, with parties bargaining to assemble the alliances needed to govern.
