articles.title: Republican AGs stand ready as 'last line of defense' against leftist policies after dismal midterms for party
articles.excerpt: Bold conservative policies and crucial ballot measures helped Florida successfully mitigate the blue 'wave' during the midterm elections. Governor Ron DeSantis discusses how his state avoided a near e...
articles.body_text:
Bold conservative policies and crucial ballot measures helped Florida successfully mitigate the blue 'wave' during the midterm elections. Governor Ron DeSantis discusses how his state avoided a near extinction level event for the Republican Party.

Republican attorney general candidates outperformed other midterm GOP hopefuls in several key races, according to a post-election analysis from the Republican Attorneys General Association, which urged colleagues to view their role as the "front line" against leftist policies following results that were likened to a "category-five political hurricane."

"America needs Republican Attorneys General now more than ever," RAGA Executive Director Adam Piper wrote in a late-night memo to colleagues shared with Fox News Digital. "With an emboldened Democrat Congress, Republican AGs are both America’s front line and is the last line of defense when it comes to their left-wing wish list – such as court packing, the Green New Deal, Medicare for All, Second Amendment restrictions, and abolishing ICE."

Piper, who has worked in Virginia and on the staff of South Carolina Gov.-elect Alan Wilson, noted midterm election results showed Republican attorneys general candidates holding up slightly better on ballots despite a difficult Tuesday night for the party.

AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

Republican midterm dissatisfaction will have a lasting impact on the party, but the executive director of the Republican Attorneys General Association is urging its colleagues to hold the "front line" against the Democrats' "category-five hurricane" of sweeping blue takeovers. (Adam Gray/Getty Images)

"Last night was the worst election night for the Republican Party in 50 years," Piper's memo began, acknowledging a difficult midterm "environment" that was ultimately made worse. "Last night, voters, regardless of party, preferred Democrat candidates by a mean of D +13.8 compared to D +7.9 in 2006 and D +8.4 in 2018.

"Today, we are dealing with the aftermath of a category-five political hurricane. It will take years to fully rebuild."

As Republicans are picking up the pieces and evaluating the map overcome with blue, even along wide swaths of Texas' southern border, the party is looking to the slight holds in Florida and any other silver linings.

Attorneys general might have something in the way of a pep talk for the party from Piper's memo.

GOP AG candidates ran an average of 4.62 percentage points ahead of GOP Senate candidates in comparable states and 2.12 points ahead of Republican gubernatorial candidates, according to the returns as of the late Wednesday night memo.

Republican AG candidates posted better margins than GOP Senate candidates in nine of 10 comparable states and outperformed Republican gubernatorial candidates in nine of 13 states, Piper wrote.

STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE

Still, Piper made clear that "there are no moral victories." Republicans did lose five AG seats to Democrats in these midterms, compared to a projected net loss of 51 in the House and a potential net loss of nine Senate seats.

Iowa, Ohio and Colorado were among the widest outperformers. The Republican attorney general candidates in those states ran 9.3, 7.3 and 10.3 points ahead of their party’s gubernatorial candidates, respectively. In Colorado, the GOP attorney general candidate also outpaced the Republican Senate candidate by 7.7 points.

FLORIDA'S DESANTIS DESCRIBES GOP MIDTERMS WIPEOUT AS 'CLOSE TO AN EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT' FOR REPUBLICANS

In Florida, now the largest red state with the handing over of Texas to the Democratic Party, Republican Attorney General James Uthmeier won by 1.8 percentage points, outperforming Gov.-elect Byron Donalds, who won by 1.3 points.

Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers won re-election by 12.6 points, compared with a 6.7-point win for Republican Senate candidate Pete Ricketts and an 8.4-point victory for Republican Gov. Jim Pillen.

RAGA spent more than $40 million on these midterms, nearly twice its spending in 2022, and was on track to raise more than $50 million, according to Piper.

"No amount of outperformance can make up for the historical Republican losses," his memo concluded. "RAGA will start to candidate recruit for 2027 and 2028 now and has set the expectation that we will continue to overperform, no matter the environment."

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

articles.title: Grocery store cyberattacks are ‘psychological warfare’ that could strike US, former FBI agent warns
articles.excerpt:
Former FBI special agent Nicole Parker says cyberattacks targeting grocery store refrigeration systems in Europe underscore the need to protect critical infrastructure.

Former FBI Special Agent Nicol...
articles.body_text:
Former FBI special agent Nicole Parker says cyberattacks targeting grocery store refrigeration systems in Europe underscore the need to protect critical infrastructure.

Former FBI Special Agent Nicole Parker warned that the next attack on Americans’ sense of security could come through the grocery aisle after suspected hackers have turned up supermarket freezer temperatures in Europe and fueled fears that everyday necessities could become weapons of "psychological warfare."

Parker warned that cyberattacks targeting the systems people rely on for food and other essentials could also strike the United States.

"Every human being has to eat," Parker told Fox News Digital. "This is the grocery store."

HACKERS COULD ALREADY BE INSIDE AMERICAN UTILITIES, CYBER EXPERTS WARN OF 'TROJAN HORSE' THREAT

Cyberattacks on supermarkets could target the U.S., according to a former FBI agent.  (iStock)

Her warning comes as the Army Criminal Investigation Division’s Cyber Field Office works with the Defense Commissary Agency and the Defense Criminal Investigative Service to determine what caused refrigeration failures at military commissaries in August, an Army CID spokesperson confirmed to Fox News Digital.

Investigators are also working with French law enforcement as they examine whether the U.S. failures could be linked to refrigeration outages in Europe. A cyberattack has not been established as the cause of the military commissary malfunctions.

MAJOR US GROCERY CHAINS HIT BY CYBERSECURITY INCIDENT

U.S. Army Fort Huachuca in August said an outage affected the base's commissaries. (U.S. Army Fort Huachuca)

At least six commissaries, grocery stores on military bases serving military personnel, experienced refrigeration problems in late August.

"ALL frozen food has spoiled," Fort Huachuca in Arizona said in an Aug. 26 Facebook post.

FOREIGN HACKERS BREACH TWO MORE US WATER UTILITIES, THREATEN SAFETY OF COLORADO RESIDENTS

Other affected locations included F.E. Warren Air Force Base in Wyoming, Naval Station Newport in Rhode Island, Columbus Air Force Base in Mississippi and Travis Air Force Base and Fort Irwin in California. Fort Irwin limited commissary sales to dry goods after its malfunction.

In at least one case, refrigeration units were set to higher temperatures overnight rather than simply shutting off, Reuters reported.

HOW FOREIGN HACKERS COULD 'CRUMBLE' AMERICA BY TARGETING ONE ESSENTIAL UTILITY

U.S. Marine Corps Sgt. Drew Jordan Pocaigue, a supply chain manager with Headquarters and Support Battalion, Marine Corps Installations West, loads a broken refrigerator onto a truck during Operation Clean Sweep II at Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton, Calif., April 3, 2025.  (U.S. Marine Corps photo by Cpl. Noah Martinez)

Separately, refrigeration systems at European supermarkets were disrupted Monday, forcing some retailers to discard food. Reuters reported that affected businesses included stores in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg, with temperatures in some systems reaching 122 degrees Fahrenheit.

Parker said the incidents underscore a threat she has long discussed with former FBI colleagues: cyberattacks targeting critical infrastructure.

AMERICA'S NEXT WAR COULD REACH US SOIL, TOP ARMY GENERAL WARNS

"What we're seeing right now is in Europe and other places, but it can very well happen on our soil," she said.

She described the danger as "asymmetrical warfare" in which an attacker can disrupt daily life without firing a missile or sending troops onto a battlefield.

AN AI CYBERATTACK COULD TURN OFF AMERICA'S LIGHTS BEFORE WASHINGTON EVEN UNDERSTANDS WHY

A young woman carries a shopping basket filled with fresh produce while shopping in a grocery store. (iStock)

"No one in law enforcement underestimates the harm that could be caused by a cyberattack against our country or against our allies," Parker said.

The identity of those behind the European incidents remained unknown, Reuters reported Wednesday. Parker also cautioned against drawing conclusions about who was responsible.

UKRAINE SAYS AIR ALERT SYSTEM HACKED AFTER FALSE RADIATION WARNING IN KYIV

"Again, we don't know who did this," she said.

For Parker, the potential damage goes beyond spoiled food. Targeting a basic necessity can also shake the public’s sense of security.

IF HACKERS CRIPPLE AMERICA'S WATER, THE CONSEQUENCES COULD BE CATASTROPHIC

"This asymmetrical warfare has a very strong psychological impact, but we're Americans. We will not falter ever," she said.

Parker said the response must extend beyond investigators tracking down hackers. Elected officials and local leaders responsible for keeping communities running need training and plans to help residents if essential services are disrupted.

"We're in a place now where it's not just enough for law enforcement to be prepared," she said.

City managers, mayors and city council members must understand potential threats and how they would take care of their communities, Parker said. She stressed the need to identify vulnerabilities and stop attacks before they happen.

Parker urged families to keep basic supplies on hand and have a plan in case a cyberattack disrupts essential services.

"I think if you are prepared, you do not have to fear," Parker said.

She encouraged Americans to keep food, water and needed medicine on hand, gather important documents in a designated location and talk about how family members would communicate during a power outage. She also suggested having a battery-operated AM radio.

"I'm not saying that, you know, you need to go buy everything off of the shelves," Parker said.

Instead, she urged people to think about practical preparations as they go about their routines.

For Parker, who lives in Florida, the approach is familiar.

"We're used to hurricanes," she said. "The preparation would be very much the same."

Fox News Digital's Bonny Chu contributed to this report.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: Paraguay President Santiago Peña resigns after bank collapse
articles.excerpt:
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has announced his resignation following a political crisis sparked by the collapse of a bank linked to him.

"I want to apologise to the people if at any point I fai...
articles.body_text:
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has announced his resignation following a political crisis sparked by the collapse of a bank linked to him.

"I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed," he said in a video message on social media. "It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me."

The crisis erupted after Ueno Bank entered an insolvency process, which froze all operations. Lawmakers accused Peña, who was a shareholder until last year in the company that owned the bank, of conflicts of interest and misconduct.

Peña has rejected suggestions of impropriety. His resignation comes after Paraguay's lower house of congress voted in favour of pursuing an impeachment trial.

In his video message posted on X, Peña said his resignation was to protect stability, social peace and democratic institutions.

Ueno Bank has said it has about three million customers, equivalent to about 60% of Paraguay's adult population.

It held pensions and some other public funds and, after its collapse earlier this week, millions could not access their accounts.

The central bank seized the digital lender, and people took to the streets protesting and demanding Peña's resignation.

A new president of the Central Bank of Paraguay has been appointed and Congress has approved a process to pay depositors.

Peña won election in 2023 representing Paraguay's ruling conservative Colorado Party, beating a centre-left challenger.

articles.title: Multiple planes diverted as bomb threats to commercial flights reported across Europe – live
articles.excerpt:
EU transport commissioner says ‘too early’ to say if bomb threats to 20 flights are linked

Tell us: have you been affected by the bomb threats?

Here is a summary of all planes reportedly affected by...
articles.body_text:
EU transport commissioner says ‘too early’ to say if bomb threats to 20 flights are linked

Tell us: have you been affected by the bomb threats?

Here is a summary of all planes reportedly affected by bomb threats this morning – with the tally currently at 25 today:

EI-DEH Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome, diverted to Evreux, France (9:55, 10:07, 10:25)

FR6410 Ryanair flight from Madrid to Sofia (10:45)

FR3606 Ryanair flight from Copenhagen to Sofia (10:45)

FR1730 Ryanair flight from London Stansted to Sofia, diverted to Plovdiv, Bulgaria (10:45)

LO235 LOT Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Brussels (10:48)

W46387 WizzAir flight from Milan Malpensa to Warsaw-Okęcie, diverted to Vienna, Austria (10:52)

AY1761 FinnAir flight from Helsinki to Rome Fiumicino (10:52).

AY 1471 FinnAir flight from Helsinki to Vienna (11:06).

U23179 easyJet flight from Glasgow to Prague (11:16, 17:00).

U25629 easyJet flight from Newcastle to Prague (11:16, 17:00).

FR7326 Ryanair flight from Dublin to Prague (11:16, 17:00).

GQ750 Sky Express flight from Athens to Prague (11:16, 17:00).

W43064 WizzAir flight from Milan-Malpensa to Bucharest (11:50).

A3552 Aegean Airlines flight from Thessaloniki to Milan-Malpensa (12:17).

FR8953 Ryanair flight from Porto to Milan-Malpensa (12:17).

IBE668 Iberia flight from Milan to Madrid (15:33)

IBE658 Iberia flight from Rome to Madrid (15:33)

UX1027 Air Europa flight from Madrid to Paris (13:37, 16:15).

JU102 Air Serbia flight from Belgrade to Bucharest (15:25, 15:54).

A3860 Aegean Airlines flight from Athens to Vienna (16:38)

LO331 LOT Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Paris (17:54).

FR901 Ryanair flight from London Stansted to Cork (18:06).

Two unidentified planes inspected at Copenhagen airport (18:16).

FR5015 Ryanair flight from Pescara to Brussels Charleroi (18:36).

Post last updated at 18:46 CET with the latest tally

Male State is a Russian far-right, ultranationalist and misogynistic movement founded in 2016 by Vladislav Pozdnyakov, initially as an online community on the social network VKontakte.

Its supporters became known for coordinating harassment campaigns against women, LGBTQ+ people and businesses that had spoken out against discrimination.

In October 2021, the Nizhny Novgorod regional court designated Male State an extremist organisation and banned its activities in Russia.

Pozdnyakov has continued to publish far-right material online and is a prominent supporter of Russia’s war in Ukraine.

On his Telegram channel, Pozdnyakov has neither commented on nor claimed responsibility for the bomb threats.

After reports from Bulgaria (17:37) and Italy (14:38) alleging links with the “Fighters of the Male State,” let’s cross to our Russia expert Pjotr Sauer for a quick explanation on the group – with big caveats that we do not really know for sure if they are involved or not.

A separate Ryanair flight from Pescara in Italy to Brussels Charleroi had to inspected after the word “bomb” was discovered scrawled on the walls of its onboard lavatory.

The airport confirmed the incident to Belgian newspaper Le Soir and broadcaster RTBF, saying a detailed inspection of all luggage and passengers confirmed no threat.

Here’s a handy map showing some of the affected flights from our visuals department.

The full list of all affected flights today is pinned at the top here.

Two aircraft were inspected at Copenhagen Airport this morning after authorities received emailed threats against them, Danish media reported, without providing details about the flights.

Both planes were later cleared to fly after investigators confirmed there was no threat, according to broadcasters DR and TV2.

A Ryanair flight from London Stansted to Cork airport was also held up on arrival in Ireland this morning after a false bomb threat.

A Cork airport spokesperson confirmed to the Guardian the airport received “an anonymous threat by phone this morning in relation to a specific flight.”

“Elevated additional secutity measures were adopted in conjunction with An Garda Síochána. Nothing of concern was identified and the flight resumed operations with a 90-minute delay. The incident has been fully stood down.”

The airport did not identify the flight, but it was named in Irish media as FR901 from London Stansted, which experienced a delay meeting the airport’s description.

This brings today’s total up to 22 and 30 for this week.

A second LOT Polish Airlines flight – this time LO331 from Warsaw Okęcie to Paris - was also caught up in today’s false bomb alerts.

Following an anonymous report, the plane was forced to stay in Warsaw for additional checks, which showed no reason for concern.

It eventually departed just over four hours late and landed safely in Paris in the early afternoon, the Guardian confirmed.

An email sent to Sofia airport during a series of hoax alerts across Europe today was signed “the fighters of the Male State,” AFP reported.

“We, the fighters of the Male State, will make history with our actions today. Your feminist regime will remember this forever. The explosion will occur in 60 minutes. Today, your skies will turn red.”

As reported earlier (14:38), similar messages were also sent to Italian airports.

While 20 false bomb threats across Europe will certainly raise concern, it is worth keeping in mind that this is just a fraction of the overall number of planes flying across the continent every day.

Some 27,400 flights were scheduled in Europe today, according to the European air traffic control agency, Eurocontrol.

The pilot of an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome that diverted to Évreux following a bomb threat (9:55, 10:07, 10:25) is being questioned by French authorities for initially refusing to land at a military base, according to media reports in France.

AFP, France24, Le Figaro and TF1 said that the pilot reportedly insisted on landing at a civilian airport, such as Beauvais or Nantes, prompting the French air force to intercept the plane with fighter jets.

He will now be “questioned under caution,” local public prosecutor Rémi Coutin told AFP.

Aer Lingus has been approached for comment.

If you are only just joining us and what to catch up on what’s on earth is going on, here is our explainer on what do we know (and what we don’t) so far.

The four flights affected at Prague airport can now be confirmed as inbound flights from Athens, Dublin, Glasgow and Newcastle (11:16, 11:58).

A spokesperson for the Prague airport, Jiří Hannich, told the Guardian that “an anonymous threat was received concerning the possible presence of explosive devices on board selected flights” arriving to Prague.

“In accordance with the Airport Emergency Plan, the Security Operations Command Center was activated under the direction of the Police of the Czech Republic.

The aircraft landed safely in Prague and were directed to remote stands.

Following their arrival, the Police of the Czech Republic conducted security searches of the aircraft for explosives, all with negative results. All passengers safely disembarked from the aircraft and received their baggage once all necessary security measures had been completed.

The situation had no significant impact on other airport operations. The threat is currently under police investigation. For this reason, we are not in a position to provide any further details.”

Global airlines body Iata has “condemned … attempts to interrupt air transport,” urging the relevant authorities to “find the origins of these hoax threats.”

“Safety is the number one priority for the industry and we take all threats seriously,” Iata’s senior vicepresident for operations, safety and security, Nick Careen said in a statement.

“Meanwhile passengers should be assured that aviation security measures will continue to ensure the highest levels of public safety,” he added.

Austrian defence ministry spokesperson Michael Bauer has confirmed that all affected flights in Austrian airspace were escorted by Eurofighters jets.

“What the Eurofighters can achieve in this scenario: They can observe the situation on site as the sole eyewitness and report any possible deviation from the flight path if the pilot has no radio connection.

If the aircraft is damaged but remains airworthy, the EF pilot can inspect the damage and provide assistance with information about the condition. Through visual contact with the pilot, they can at least support them in any case.”

In a separate post, he confirmed there were three affected flights, which checks out with our tally (11:01).

articles.title: Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half-brother ‘person of interest’ in child sexual abuse inquiry
articles.excerpt:
Philippine official says there are ‘signs that point to Thomas Markle Jr’s involvement in crime’, but he’s not yet being treated as a suspect

The Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half-brother, Thomas Ma...
articles.body_text:
Philippine official says there are ‘signs that point to Thomas Markle Jr’s involvement in crime’, but he’s not yet being treated as a suspect

The Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, has been named as a “person of interest” in the Philippine authorities’ inquiry into child sexual abuse image allegations made against her father, Thomas Markle Sr.

The country’s interior and local government secretary, Jonvic Remulla, told a press conference in Manila there were “signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well”.

He added that Markle Jr, 60, who alerted local police and the FBI to images he found in his father’s belongings, was not yet being treated as a suspect. His alleged involvement is not thought to be directly linked to the material he handed to the police.

More than 7,000 photos and one video – all of under-age males and females of Asian, Latin and European descent, with some as young as 10 and 11 – were uncovered, Remulla said.

He described the images as “the most deplorable displays of impunity towards sexual activity that I have ever seen”.

Markle Sr, 82, who is estranged from Meghan, has reportedly been moved into a care home for dementia patients in the US where he is now living.

Remulla said: “We’re determining if [the] son is involved … There are signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well but only as a person of interest so far.”

He added: “We will know in the next few days.”

Markle Sr, who returned to the US from the Philippines in May, has admitted paying for sex in the Philippines but he has strongly denied possessing child abuse imagery, and suggested he had been “set up”. His son remains in Cebu City in the Philippines.

Remulla has previously described Markle Sr as “a possible sex offender of the grossest kind”.

Markle Jr reported his father after claiming to have found four storage boxes at his father’s home in the Philippines containing “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images.

Police and FBI agents have since been investigating whether Markle Sr was in possession of any illegal images while living in the Philippines and in Mexico, where he previously lived, and where other illegal images were reportedly found in one of his storage units.

Markle Jr was recently interviewed at his home in Cordova, Cebu, as part of an international, multi-agency meeting via Microsoft Teams, according to the Sun, which first published the claims. He gave his statement to an FBI agent based in Florida, who specialises in child sex abuse cases.

In a statement issued when the allegations against her father were first published, Meghan said she was “deeply distressed” by the claims. She said she had been informed of disturbing allegations against her father in 2018 and had kept him from having contact with her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, to protect them.

articles.title: Bomb threats disrupt at least 22 flights across Europe, raising hybrid war fears
articles.excerpt:
Planes forced into emergency landings or diversions two days after hoax alerts affected air travel

Bomb threats have caused diversions and emergency landings for at least 22 flights across Europe, re...
articles.body_text:
Planes forced into emergency landings or diversions two days after hoax alerts affected air travel

Bomb threats have caused diversions and emergency landings for at least 22 flights across Europe, renewing questions about a possibly coordinated effort to disrupt travel.

The series of warnings on Thursday affected flights between Italy, Ireland, the UK, Spain, Bulgaria, Romania, Poland, Finland, Austria, Denmark, Belgium, Portugal, France, Greece, Serbia  and Czechia.

On Tuesday seven planes across Europe were searched or diverted after malicious hoax bomb alerts. On Monday a flight from the UK to Bulgaria was diverted after a threat that was apparently without substance.

The bomb threats on Thursday affected flights by Ryanair, Aer Lingus, Wizz Air, Finnair, easyJet, Aegean Airlines, Iberia, Sky Express, Air Serbia and LOT. All landed safely. Searches of the planes found nothing suspicious.

The global airlines body Iata condemned the disruption and urged authorities to identify the origin of the threats. “Safety is the number one priority for the industry and we take all threats seriously,” said Nick Careen, Iata’s senior vice-president for operations, safety and security, in a statement.

There is no intelligence yet pointing to any particular group or state actor, such as Russia or Iran, amid growing concerns over hybrid incidents targeting Europe.

The EU transport commissioner, Apostolos Tzitzikostas, said it was too early to know if the incidents were linked but that any threats against civilians were unacceptable.

Bomb threats emailed to airports in Rome and Sofia were signed “fighters of the Male State”, according to sources at Aeroporti di Roma (ADR), which manages the city’s two airports, and a text seen by Agence France-Presse. “We, the fighters of the Male State, will make history with our actions today. Your feminist regime will remember this forever. The explosion will occur in 60 minutes. Today, your skies will turn red,” it said.

The affected flights had knock-on effects but were a tiny fraction of the 27,400 flights scheduled in Europe on Thursday, according to the European air traffic control agency, Eurocontrol.

The pilot of an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome that diverted to Évreux was being questioned by French authorities for initially refusing to land at a military base, according to French media reports.

The disruption followed cyber-attacks this week against supermarket refrigeration systems.

A Kremlin spokesperson said on Thursday it was “absurd” to blame Vladimir Putin’s administration for the fridge hacks. “We have ​such baseless accusations against our country, implicating it in everything,” Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

Many of the affected flights were operated by low-cost carriers but there was little discernible pattern surrounding the incidents.

Aviation experts say fake threats occur daily but that such a number of credible threats, even if malicious hoaxes, appears to point to coordinated action.

Capt Martin Drake, a former airline pilot and technical adviser to the Balpa union, said airlines had security teams who assessed each threat on a traffic-light scale: green to keep going or red to be grounded, with an amber option only for flights yet to take off, allowing tighter checks and searches of the plane before clearing it to fly.

“If you want to deliberately disrupt a flight, then you need to do so once it’s airborne,” said Drake. Pilots have a QRH – a quick response handbook – whose instructions will probably include to descend quickly as well as divert to the nearest airport on receipt of a red alert.

At cruising altitude, “aircraft pressurisation would do a lot of the work of any improvised explosive device”.

While getting a large explosive onboard should be ruled out by multiple layers of security and screening, the effects of any detonation would be multiplied for planes at typical cruising altitude of 35,000ft.

Diversions are expensive as well as highly disruptive, but airlines have little choice in the face of any remotely credible threat.

The ready availability of airline operations information on the internet means that any hoaxer now has a level of detail about the schedules, the type of plane and its technical specifications that would have eluded all but insiders decades ago.

Rhys Jones, an analyst at Osprey Flight Solutions, an aviation intelligence firm, said the confidence of airlines in European airport security should not mean any change to normal protocols after the hoaxes, but “one of the natural responses will be to see double-downed security, media coverage and public concern about travelling”.

He said the threats seemed linked but “a reasonably chaotic campaign with no particular region targeted”, and while they could weaken future security responses through the normalisation of threats, simply creating disruption could be regarded as a success by those carrying out the hoaxes.

articles.title: Nasdaq heading for worst day in 18 months as Wall Street sustains widespread losses
articles.excerpt:
Share index slumps 5% amid signs AI industry will face tougher regulation after Democrats’ midterm elections success

The tech-heavy US Nasdaq share index is on track for its worst day in 18 months af...
articles.body_text:
Share index slumps 5% amid signs AI industry will face tougher regulation after Democrats’ midterm elections success

The tech-heavy US Nasdaq share index is on track for its worst day in 18 months after slumping by up to 5% on Thursday amid growing signs that the artificial intelligence industry will face tougher regulation after this week’s midterm elections.

As Wall Street sustained widespread losses, the Nasdaq composite tumbled into ‘correction territory’ – more than 10% below its recent record high. The index was heading for its biggest one-day fall since Donald Trump announced his ‘liberation day’ tariffs on US trading partners in April 2025.

Worries over massive AI spending gripped the New York stock market and rippled out to other bourses worldwide as investors anticipated tougher scrutiny of datacentre expansion plans.

Chip stocks led the slump, with memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 19% and hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 16.5%.

Wall Street’s ‘fear index’, the VIX, jumped by 40% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.

Analysts pointed to expectations that Democratic governors will clamp down on the rollout of new datacentres after the party won a series of gubernatorial races this week. US voters also rejected datacentres in a series of local ballots about the issue across the country.

Neil Wilson, investor strategist at Saxo UK, said a “complete capitulation level event” was playing out in tech stocks on Thursday.

“The fear is a total momentum unwind as Democrats pace the frontier and kibosh datacentre buildout … this looks totally overdone but the nature of ‘sell everything’ in this market means we need to look for some stability first,” Wilson said.

The Dow Jones industrial average (DJIA) of 30 large US companies was down more than 1,000 points in late morning trading, a fall of 2%, to 52,264 points.

Nvidia, the chipmaker at the heart of the AI boom, was the top faller on the DJIA – down 6.7%, followed by Goldman Sachs, which fell 5.7%.

The sell-off is a sharp reversal on Wednesday’s rally, when Wall Street stocks had their biggest daily gain in months as investors anticipated that the Democratic party’s success in the US midterm elections could restrain the White House.

Tech analyst Dan Ives has warned that the results of the midterms are a clear sign that the pace of datacentre buildout will start to slow down.

“There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control, especially over the Senate, will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next two years,” Ives said.

An early stock market rally in Europe had fizzled out by late trading, with Britain’s FTSE 100 closing down 46 points or 0.4% at 10782.66.

articles.title: Henry Nowak’s killer has sentence extended by court of appeal
articles.excerpt:
Vickrum Digwa’s ‘unduly lenient’ term for Southampton teenager’s murder increased after attorney general’s appeal

Henry Nowak’s killer has seen his sentence extended by the court of appeal after it r...
articles.body_text:
Vickrum Digwa’s ‘unduly lenient’ term for Southampton teenager’s murder increased after attorney general’s appeal

Henry Nowak’s killer has seen his sentence extended by the court of appeal after it ruled that his original sentence was “unduly lenient”.

Vickrum Digwa’s original sentence of life with a minimum term of 21 years was lengthened to a minimum of 24 years and 190 days after a successful appeal by the attorney general, Ellie Reeves.

Digwa, 23, stabbed Nowak several times in an attack in Southampton in December last year.

When police arrived at the murder scene, Digwa falsely claimed Nowak had racially abused him and knocked his turban off, causing officers to arrest and handcuff Nowak before they saw his fatal injuries.

Digwa filmed his victim as he lay dying and lied to emergency services that Nowak, 18, had racially abused him.

The incident led to riots in Southampton.

Lady Chief Justice Carr said the original sentencing judge, William Mousley KC, had materially understated two distinct dimensions of Digwa’s offending.

She said: “First, the circumstances in which a large and immediately available dagger was used repeatedly with an intention to kill an unarmed man, and secondly, the deliberate cruelty, additional suffering, and obstruction [of justice] which followed the stabbing.”

She added: “A minimum term of 21 years did not adequately reflect the overall seriousness of the murder. It was not only lenient, but unduly so.

“Therefore, we quash the minimum term of 21 years. We replace it with a minimum term of 25 years. From that term must be deducted the 175 days spent in custody on remand, producing an operative minimum term of 24 years and 190 days.”

In written submissions on behalf of Reeves, Jonathan Polnay KC said the sentence failed to take into account a series of “significant aggravating factors”, including Digwa’s “false allegation of racism against the deceased” and his “abuse” of the privilege afforded to Sikhs to carry a knife in a public place for religious reasons.

At Digwa’s sentencing hearing, Mousley said that on the night of the murder, Digwa had a small knife hidden from view called a kirpan, which is a strict requirement for Sikhs to carry at all times.

Digwa also had a “large dagger in a sheath” due to his membership of the Nihang, an order of Sikhs which has a tradition of holding a second knife.

Polnay told the court that the attempt to increase the sentence was “not about the lawful possession of a kirpan” and the laws allowing Sikhs to carry blades. “It is about what followed.” He said Digwa’s use of the dagger was “on at least one level, analogous to an abuse of trust”.

He continued: “When a person who has the benefit of that accommodation uses the article protected by law for repeated lethal violence, that is an aggravating factor of particular weight.”

Polnay also cited “the offender’s sustained attempts to pervert the course of justice” and “his procurement of his mother’s assistance in concealing evidence”.

Digwa’s mother, Kiran Kaur, 53, was jailed for three years for assisting an offender by taking the knife from where her son murdered Novak back to the family home.

Polnay said other aggravating factors included Digwa’s “degradation of the dying victim by filming him, and his conduct in misleading responders”.

His submission said: “The minimum term imposed failed adequately to reflect the combined weight of those features.”

In her ruling made alongside Mr Justice Nicklin and Mr Justice Wall, Carr said: “A person who knowingly carries a large knife or other bladed article in public, even if lawfully, and then uses it to kill an unarmed man after only a brief altercation, is highly culpable. His culpability is much closer to that of a person who takes a weapon into the street for offensive use than to that of someone who kills without a weapon, or someone who picks up a weapon of opportunity.”

On the false allegations of racism, Carr said: “It is unnecessary for us to determine whether the allegation of racial abuse was false, for even if that finding is left out of account, it does not affect our assessment of the appropriate minimum term.”

Digwa watched proceedings from HMP Frankland in County Durham, wearing a dark suit, shirt and tie.

Members of Nowak’s family attended the hearing at the Royal Courts of Justice, with one relative wiping their eyes as the ruling was handed down.

Imran Khan KC, for Digwa, said the sentence could be increased only in “exceptional, rather than borderline cases, and directed to gross error by the sentencing judge”. He asked: “Where is the gross error?”

Challenging the length of the sentence, Khan said that while Digwa’s lies to first responders “unquestionably affected the dignity with which Mr Nowak was treated”, his wounds were unsurvivable. “The false account therefore did not worsen the fatal injury or deprive Mr Nowak of the prospect of survival,” he said.

In response to Digwa’s appeal, Carr said: “Having reached the conclusion that the proper minimum term would be at least 25 years, we refuse Digwa leave to appeal against his sentence. It is unarguable that it is manifestly excessive.”

Reeves said: “The brutality and cruelty of this case horrified me, and I know that feeling is shared by the British public. I welcome the court of appeal’s decision to increase the minimum term of Digwa’s life sentence.”

articles.title: Harmeet Dhillon, controversial head of DoJ’s civil rights division, reportedly steps down
articles.excerpt:
Dhillon is first high-level justice department official to leave after historic Republican defeat in 2026 midterms

Harmeet Dhillon, a Donald Trump ally who led the justice department’s civil rights d...
articles.body_text:
Dhillon is first high-level justice department official to leave after historic Republican defeat in 2026 midterms

Harmeet Dhillon, a Donald Trump ally who led the justice department’s civil rights division, is leaving her position.

“Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division with conviction the past 18 months. She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor. The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors,” the attorney general, Todd Blanche, said in a post on X.

Dhillon is the first high-ranking justice department official to leave after the midterm elections in which Democrats took control of Congress. Democrats are expected to use that power to aggressively investigate executive agencies, including the justice department. Dhillon’s departure was first reported by Bloomberg Law.

Dhillon dramatically transformed the civil rights division in a little over a year and a half there, reorienting its mission away from the work it had traditionally done protecting the civil rights of minorities. Under her leadership, the department dropped many cases alleging discrimination against racial minorities in voting, housing, employment and education. Scores of career lawyers also left the division under her leadership, leading to an exodus of expertise of civil rights enforcement.

Dhillon aggressively pursued claims of discrimination at universities, including claims that minorities were unfairly favored in admissions and claims of antisemitism against Jewish students. A whistleblower has said that investigations into the schools were conducted with a predetermined outcome and that lawyers were told to find a reason to file a lawsuit.

The civil rights division also oversaw investigations into the killing of US citizens Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good by federal agents in Minnesota during an immigration enforcement surge – neither has resulted in criminal charges.

The division also had some high-profile failures under Dhillon’s watch. It sued more than two dozen states for voter roll information and lost every single case. Several of the judges who ruled against the department were appointed by Donald Trump,

“Harmeet Dhillon has been the most destructive, lawless and hateful head of the civil rights division in DoJ history,” said Stacey Young, a former civil rights division lawyer who now leads the group Justice Connection, a group for justice department alumni.

She added: “After she upended the division’s mission-critical work, the civil servants who dedicated their careers to protecting vulnerable communities were instead told to target them – and more than three-quarters of the division’s lawyers left. Dhillon wielded the enormous power of the justice department to threaten universities, state and local officials, and election workers in spurious cases that rarely won in court.”

A prolific poster on X, Dhillon would sometimes reveal civil rights investigations on the platform, a move that startled longtime justice department lawyers because the department has a longstanding practice of not speaking publicly about investigations. She has also publicly used a slur for people with disabilities, whose civil rights her division is charged with protecting. She has also described conservative influencers as “hoes”.

Dhillon grew up in Smithfield, North Carolina, after being born in India and then living in the UK and New York. “There were Klan signs on the highway where I grew up. I’m used to being an outsider. My superpower is not really caring what people think about me,” she told the Dartmouth alumni magazine last year.

Before joining the government, Dhillon ran her own law firm and was vice-chair of the California GOP. After the 2020 election, she worked on lawsuits contesting the election results.

articles.title: US elections 2026 live: Republicans blast their party’s midterms collapse, blaming Iran war and affordability crisis
articles.excerpt:
Democrats widen gap in House chamber by flipping more seats; Ted Cruz call the US midterms election a ‘Watergate-level repudiation’

Live results | How do you feel about the results?

Democrats have p...
articles.body_text:
Democrats widen gap in House chamber by flipping more seats; Ted Cruz call the US midterms election a ‘Watergate-level repudiation’

Live results | How do you feel about the results?

Democrats have picked-up four more House seats, adding to their new majority. As things stand, the party has 247 seats in the lower chamber, with 35 races left to be called. Here are some of the Democrats’ latest pick-ups.

Montana’s first congressional district: Here Democrat Sam Forstag, a 32-year-old smoke jumper, beat Republican Aaron Flint, a conservative radio host. The seat is currently held by the two-term GOP representative Ryan Zinke.

Arizona’s first congressional district: Amish Shah, a Democrat and emergency room doctor, won a district held by Republican David Schweikert, who launched an unsuccessful bid for Arizona governor. Shah won the seat, which includes parts of Phoenix and Scottsdale, against GOP nominee Jay Freely, a former NFL player.

North Carolina’s sixth congressional district: Democratic state representative Cyril Jefferson beat Republican incumbent Addison McDowell – who won the seat by nearly 40 points in 2024, after it was successfully gerrymandered to benefit the GOP.

North Carolina’s 13th congressional district: Here, Democrat Paul Barringer, an attorney, defeated the first-term Republican incumbent Brad Knott. The district was also redrawn ahead of the 2024 to boost Republicans, after Democrats flipped the seat in 2022.

Harmeet Dhillon, the justice department lawyer who leads the Civil Rights division, is planning to resign, according to Bloomberg.

Citing four people familiar with the matter, Bloomberg reports that Dhillon has told allies that she would leave the DoJ after the midterm elections.

The justice department did not immediately respond to the Guardian’s request for comment on the matter.

As my colleague Sam Levine reports, Dhillon – who once worked as Donald Trump’s personal lawyer – oversees the justice department division responsible for enforcing America’s federal civil rights laws. Since arriving at the justice department in April 2025, Dhillon has dropped dozens of anti-discrimination cases seeking relief for minorities in voting, housing, policing and employment and instead reorienting the division around preventing discrimination against white Americans. Hundreds of attorneys have left the division.

Dhillon made her name in Maga circles by taking on culture-war cases as a San Francisco lawyer and became a fixture in rightwing media, appearing often on Fox shows. She has filed various lawsuits over election “integrity” issues and supported Trump’s quests to overturn results in 2020.

Voters in Washington state have passed a ballot measure banning transgender girls from playing on girls’ sports teams, a major loss for LGBTQ+ rights in a solidly Democratic state.

The measure says students in elementary, middle and high school who want to join girls’ athletics must first submit statements from their healthcare providers verifying their “biological sex”. Opponents have raised alarms the measure may force girls to endure “invasive and extreme” genital exams to participate in school sports.

Initiative 638 passed with support from nearly 57% of voters as of Thursday morning, though votes were still being counted.

More than 25 states across the US have adopted similar bans on trans youth athletes, mostly through legislation pushed by Republican lawmakers. Voters in Arizona and Nebraska approved similar ballot measures this week, and a ban proposed in Colorado was leading in early results, but that race has not yet been called.

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senator-elect in Michigan, said that the new majority in the upper chamber needs “action” from their leader, in an interview in CNN.

On the campaign trail, El-Sayed refused to back Senator Chuck Schumer, who currently serves as the minority leader. Schumer initially backed El-Sayed’s opponent, Congresswoman Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary, before supporting El-Sayed in the general election and blasting Stevens for her “despicable betrayal” in endorsing Republican Mike Rogers.

Speaking to CNN, El-Sayed reiterated that Senator Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat, would be an “amazing Senate majority leader”, but didn’t completely rule out supporting Schumer.

“It seems like [Van Hollen] is quite interested in another goal politically, which, you know, would mean that would be very difficult for him to do that,” El-Sayed said, referring to reports about the Senator’s presidential ambitions. “A vote is a choice between two or more options. I don’t know what those options are. But here’s what I’ll say. We need action.”

double quotation markI don’t know who’s stepping up and saying, I want to be Senate majority leader … if we have another option, I’m going to look at that and say, who is best placed to get us action, to get money out of politics, put money in pockets, pass Medicare for All.

The tech industry spent big on the midterms, but it turned out to be a poor investment. Elon Musk poured a staggering $446m dollars into Republican-aligned political action committees (Pacs) and groups since last year, but his efforts didn’t pay off. Democrats won every one of the five Senate races where Musk’s America Pac spent the most money backing Republican candidates.

In today’s episode our Stateside podcast Carter Sherman and Kai Wright are joined by the Guardian’s US tech editor, Blake Montgomery, to ask what the “blue tsunami” will mean for Musk and the wider tech industry. Will this spell the end of AI datacenters? And if so, what could this mean for the US economy?

There are “knives out” at the Pentagon as Trump administration officials reel from the thrashing dealt to the GOP in this week’s midterms – and Trump is looking for someone to blame after his unpopular war on Iran sealed the party’s fate, according to the Washington Post (paywall) this morning.

According to the Post’s sources, rather than place blame with his defense secretary Pete Hegseth, Trump could be more likely to instead sack General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, or Admiral Brad Cooper, who has overseen the war.

Hegseth has survived many a controversy in his short tenure, a number of which – from Signal-gate to alleged potential war crimes – many thought should’ve been career-ending. But he has held Trump’s confidence time and time again, including after reports that he misled the president over the course of the war.

I’m at the US Capitol, where there’s not a lot going on, since lawmakers are not scheduled to reconvene until next week.

But the good vibes Democrats are feeling after their dramatic victories in Tuesday’s midterm elections are real, particularly in deep-blue Washington DC.

A shirtless man just jogged by, pointing at the Capitol and yelling, “we got it back!” A group of what looked like visiting students cheered with him.

Joining the chorus of Republicans – who have blasted their party’s poor performance in the midterms – is sitting senator Ted Cruz, of Texas, who said the GOP were handed an “ass-kicking” this cycle, losing control of Congress.

“It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election, it was a Watergate-level repudiation,” he said on an episode of his podcast, ‘The Verdict’.

He noted, like vice-president JD Vance, that there wasn’t a turnout issue. “Instead, our voters Republicans, Libertarians, Independents, showed up and voted and rejected our candidates, voting Democrat,” Cruz said, noting that economic anxiety appeared to be top of mind this cycle.

“Food is too high, gas is too high, diesel is too high, insurance is too high, life is too high,” he added. “Too many Republican politicians seem like they didn’t understand or they didn’t care.”

Cruz, who is up for re-election in 2030 is also a contender as a Republican candidate for president.

“We need to listen and respond. We need to champion economic policies that make a real difference in working people’s lives, and we need to deal with the consequences,” Cruz added, noting that he called Democratic senator-elect James Talarico to congratulate him on his victory.

Newt Gingrich, the former Republican House speaker and fierce ally of Donald Trump, excoriated his party on social media, as the autopsies of the GOP performance in the November midterms continue.

“The American people were angrier over their own pocketbooks than they were worried about socialism or Islam,” Gingrich wrote on social media. “They wanted to send a message and boy did they ever.”

Gingrich added: “This was a failed performance election and that reality overwhelmed virtually everything else.”

It’s a direct rebuke the campaign rhetoric used by the administration on the campaign trail, that pushed racist tropes and unfounded allegations about several candidates, and largely ignored the impact of the Iran war prices.

The blue wave that swept Republicans out of power across the United States didn’t just strike Congress. In Tuesday’s midterm elections, Democrats gained hundreds of seats in state legislatures across the country, under-the-radar victories that may have major implications for life in America.

Though ballots are still being counted, the party’s success appear to be historic – Democrats haven’t won full control of government in Arizona in 60 years, in Pennsylvania since the 1990s, and Wisconsin since their wipeout in 2010. In Michigan and Minnesota, they regained trifectas they lost after the 2024 election, while in Texas, they will control the state house for the first time since 2002.

The victories are so comprehensive that majorities of Americans are set to live in states with a Democratic governor, and in several states where the party has been locked out of power for years, if not decades, Democrats are expected to embark on aggressive legislative sprees that will have implications nationwide.

“This was the most significant night for state legislative power since the seismic Republican wave in 2010,” said Mandara Meyers, the executive director of the States Project, which supported Democratic seeking state legislative office in the midterms.

The result of their efforts, Meyers said, was the inverse of that pivotal election 16 years ago, when Republicans took over a host of states, then redrew congressional and state legislative maps to prolong their power while enacting conservative laws that linger to this day.

One of the House races we’re watching, that would be evidence of another Democratic flip in the lower chamber, is Colorado’s fourth congressional district.

Democrat Eileen Laubacher is hoping to beat Republican incumbent and Maga firebrand Lauren Boebert.

Libertarian Douglas Mangeris also has about 3% of the vote.

As of now, with more than 95% of ballots counted, Laubacher is leading by more than 2,000 votes. Returns also show that the district has swung by 19 points for Democrats, compared to the 2024 race where Boebert won re-election.

As we continue watching for the remaining results in two US Senate races (Mississippi and Alaska), and several House contests, it’s worth noting that Donald Trump has no events open to the press today.

The president will be in Washington and spend the day in closed-door meetings. We’ll keep an eye on anything opening up last minute. On Wednesday we had an impromptu appearance from Trump as he showed the media around the site of his new White House ballroom project – with little mention of the Republican drubbing in the midterms that saw his party lose control of both chambers of Congress.

With many seats still to come in, the Democrats have taken control of the Senate, House and several key governorships. Find live updating results in full here:

Reproductive rights were on the ballot on Tuesday night as voters weighed in on several abortion-related measures, delivering a largely successful night for reproductive rights advocates encompassed by a historic blue wave.

In Nevada, voters approved an amendment enshrining abortion rights in the state constitution, permanently protecting access to abortion through the second trimester after a second referendum on the measure.

Virginia voters also approved a constitutional amendment establishing a “fundamental right to reproductive freedom”.

This measure also protects access to abortion during the first two trimesters of pregnancy. It permits government regulation in the third trimester while preserving access to abortion when necessary to protect the life or health of the pregnant woman. The amendment also establishes rights to contraception and fertility care, among other protections.

In Missouri, voters rejected an effort to overturn the constitutional right to reproductive freedom they had approved in 2024. Amendment 3, which would have repealed those protections, restricted abortion, and prohibited gender transition surgeries and certain other procedures for minors, failed by a margin of 55% to 45%.

The proposal, placed on the ballot by the Republican-led legislature, would have banned abortion except in cases of rape and incest during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, or later in cases involving fetal anomalies.

Meanwhile, voters in Idaho, one of the nation’s most conservative states, rejected an effort to repeal the state’s abortion ban. The result leaves in place Idaho’s abortion restrictions, which took effect in 2022 following the US supreme court’s decision to overturn Roe v Wade, ending the nationwide constitutional right to abortion.

Ghalibaf also had a message for JD Vance this morning.

Responding to the US vice-president’s lengthy post on X, in which he blamed the Republicans’ heavy midterm losses on the war with Iran, the Iranian parliamentary speaker fired back:

double quotation markLosing gambler energy, can’t walk away from the table. Boss is prepping the next war phase while America teeters on an Israel-First cliff. Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?”

An image of Iranians burning a banner bearing Donald Trump’s image captures the depth of anti-US sentiment in Tehran, as Iranian officials seize on the midterm election results as a political rebuke to the US president.

Iranian parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf described the election outcome as a rejection of the US-Israeli war on Iran, writing on X: “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.”

Crowds gathered in Tehran’s Enghelab square last night to observe the burning of the poster which also featured US vice-president JD Vance, special envoy Steve Witkoff and Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

While Trump acknowledged that the Iran war played a part in his party’s electoral defeat, he told reporters: “I would have done it again.”

The photo of Silicon Valley centi-billionaires at Donald Trump’s inauguration – Musk, Bezos, and Zuckerberg, front row and side by side – now looks like a hitlist for a blue Congress hellbent on making life difficult for billionaires.

The picture symbolized at the time the bending of the knee by the richest men in the world to its most powerful, a symbiosis of the ultra-rich. Already unfathomably wealthy, Silicon Valley tycoons believed a Maga-sized public shift to the right would enrich them even more. It did. For several years, while Trump seemed an everlasting kingmaker and AI’s expansion seemed unstoppable, their fortunes ballooned to values beyond comprehension. Elon Musk’s surpassed $1tn.

In the harsh blue light of Tuesday’s midterms, though, going all-in on Maga seems an unwisely unhedged bet. Democrats took decisive control of the US Congress, flipping seats right and left that in previous years seemed like given wins for Republicans. Governors’ mansions across the country likewise lit up blue as Democrats ascended even in the reddest of states, such as Texas.

Voters concerned about corruption expressed their displeasure at oligarchs’ blatant attempts to create a political environment to their liking. Voting against technocrats drove people into the hands of Democrats and away from Republicans. Tech oligarchs themselves, along with anger over the AI boom, datacenters and Flock surveillance cameras, shifted the tides.

“Voters rejected Republicans in part because they were bought and paid for by AI billionaires. Democrats must hold them accountable instead of cashing their checks,” wrote Texas Democratic representative Greg Casar.

The president of Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has welcomed the Democrats’ sweeping victory in the midterm elections, expressing hope that the shift in Congress could translate into greater US support for his country.

Speaking to German broadcaster ZDF, he said the Democratic party has been clear about its commitment to supporting Ukraine and strengthening ties between Washington and Europe.

double quotation markI am also grateful to the Republicans, but the Democrats speak very clearly about supporting Ukraine, about providing aid to Ukraine. They speak of renewing the ties between the US and Europe… That is why there is hope that a balance of power will be achieved and that we will receive more support.”

double quotation markIf Congress now speaks of strong financial support or military aid, just as Europe is doing and demonstrating today, then that will be a positive development that will influence [Vladimir] Putin.”

articles.title: Beware ‘sun, sea and surgery’ cosmetic tourism packages, experts advise
articles.excerpt:
British College of Aesthetic Medicine launches checklist as part of ‘vet it before you get it’ campaign

Cosmetic tourism is often sold as a package of sun, sea and surgery, but experts have said trav...
articles.body_text:
British College of Aesthetic Medicine launches checklist as part of ‘vet it before you get it’ campaign

Cosmetic tourism is often sold as a package of sun, sea and surgery, but experts have said travelling overseas for procedures can end in infections, disfigurement and death.

Nora Nugent, a consultant plastic surgeon and former president of the British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons, said travelling to countries such as Turkey for surgery came with myriad risks – and not just on the operating table.

“Actually, the risks start from the moment you step on the plane to after you return home, and until you’re fully healed and you’re out of the clotting risk time,” she said, noting that travel itself could increase the risks of clots. A lack of in-person aftercare is also a concern.

The British College of Aesthetic Medicine has launched a checklist as part of its “vet it before you get it” campaign, intended to help potential patients make better and safer choices about overseas cosmetic surgery.

As well as setting out red flags to look out for, the campaign suggests those seeking cosmetic surgery independently verify a surgeon’s qualifications, determine what emergency facilities are available near the chosen clinic and find out what insurance the practitioner has in place.

Nugent said a major driver for patients seeking procedures in countries such as Turkey was their relative cheapness, but that prices were high in the UK as a result of factors including the higher cost of living and higher fees for medical indemnity and insurance.

Chrissie Wolfe, the founder and chief executive of Lupa Law, a specialist medical negligence practice, said there could be a host of difficulties in making a claim should a procedure go wrong overseas, and that even if compensation were awarded, it could be far lower than in the UK.

“Turkey is the most popular destination by far for cosmetic surgery, but it is absolutely the most difficult from a legal perspective,” she said. “When something goes wrong, it’s incredibly difficult to put right.”

She said those looking to undergo cosmetic surgery abroad should be wary of clinics selling bundles of procedures or time-limited deals, noting that one patient had gone to Turkey for a tummy tuck but was upsold a “mummy makeover” that included a breast uplift.

“She came back and had a very severe infection,” she said. “She ultimately ended up losing most of her left breast and the entire right breast on a procedure that she didn’t even want in the first place.”

Wolfe said the marketing of travelling abroad for cosmetic surgery as a glossy holiday was problematic. “It shifts the patient’s mind away from the seriousness of what they’re actually embarking on,” she said.

It is not the first time overseas cosmetic surgery has sparked warnings. The then health secretary, Wes Streeting, urged caution over such procedures in 2024.

Data, however, suggests growing numbers of residents in Great Britain are travelling overseas for medical treatment. According to data from the Office for National Statistics, about 524,000 did so in 2024, including cosmetic procedures, up from 431,000 in 2023.

Brazillian butt lifts (BBLs) have the highest risk of death, but other overseas procedures have also left patients with problems.

Nugent cited the case of a woman who had developed abscesses and infections in her neck after a facelift. She needed long-term antibiotics and drainage procedures and was left with significant scarring.

Another woman in her late 20s had a breast lift and labiaplasty abroad after pregnancy. She ended up with a loss of tissue on one breast, her implant exposed and over-reduced labia. As a result she needed corrective surgeries, including to redo the lifts and improve the labiaplasty.

“But you can’t get things back to how they were,” said Nugent.

A third woman underwent a tummy tuck overseas, she said, but the wound came apart and required surgical cleaning. She has been left with scarring and a dip in her tummy.

“These are three examples of patients who suffered fairly horrific complications from procedures that were meant to improve how they looked and how they felt about themselves and have ended up doing exactly the opposite,” Nugent said.

articles.title: K-pop group NewJeans’s contract omitted rights to ‘sleep and free choice’ – report
articles.excerpt:
New report finds that record label Ador stripped child protections from group’s contracts when they were minors

The superstar K-pop group NewJeans signed restrictive record label contracts that waive...
articles.body_text:
New report finds that record label Ador stripped child protections from group’s contracts when they were minors

The superstar K-pop group NewJeans signed restrictive record label contracts that waived their right to “sleep, rest and free choice”.

A new report from the New York Times found that the contracts were signed when the members of the record-breaking girl group were aged 14 to 17.

The contracts banned the performers from having an “insincere attitude” and engaging in “inappropriate romantic relationships”. They also struck standard child protection language which protected “basic human rights” including the group members’ right to education.

The contracts from record label Ador (a subsidiary of Hybe, home of popular groups BTS and Katseye) additionally excluded portions of the Korean government’s K-pop contract template stipulating that the label “shall not demand that a performer who is a minor engage in excessive physical exposure or overly sexually suggestive expression”.

In a statement to the New York Times, Hybe representatives said the company adheres to child-protection laws and works hard to make sure its artists work and train in safe conditions.

NewJeans are one of the decade’s most popular K-pop acts. In 2023, the five-member group followed Blackpink to become the second Korean girl-group to score a number one album on the Billboard charts. In November 2024, the band made global headlines when they announced their decision to leave the label amid contract disputes and claims that Ador had deliberately undermined their careers.

Band member Hanni alleged that NewJeans were mistreated by the label and accused Ador of “deliberate miscommunications and manipulation” in a statement to South Korea’s parliament last year.

Ador has consistently maintained that they did not violate their duty. “A unilateral claim that trust has been broken does not constitute valid grounds for termination of a contract,” the label said in a statement.

The label sued band member Danielle, a member of her family and the band’s producer in December 2025 for a total of nearly $30m for damages and a contract break penalty.

Hybe representatives told the New York Times that its exit penalty fees do not exceed industry standards.

In July, the group promised that 2026 would be the “summer of NewJeans,” with a teaser showing the group as a four-piece sans Danielle. New music has yet to emerge.

The new reports expose the shadowy world of K-pop contracts and shine a light on the restrictive conditions that the genre’s biggest stars can be subject to.

By the time they signed their contracts, the NewJeans members – Minji, Hanni, Haerin, Hyein and Danielle – had already clocked in years of training in K-pop “boot camps” which taught vocal training, choreography and foreign language education.

Schedules were strict, one source told the New York Times, and it was not unusual for rehearsals to stretch as late as 2am. NewJeans’s youngest member, Hyein, was 12 at the time.

After the band members received their exclusive contracts with Ador in January 2022, the parents of one member requested multiple changes. They were told that the “contract itself” could be reconsidered if it was not signed in its current form.

In a statement to the New York Times, Hybe said its contracts were legal and negotiated in good faith, with protections in place for the artist as well as the label’s investment in them.

That contract also struck government language that forbade performers working for “excessive periods of time”. It also stipulated that the band would have to repay a significant percentage of the plastic surgery costs that are common in K-pop.

“We do not even recommend cosmetic surgery or procedures against an individual’s wishes,” Hybe said in a statement.

The NewJeans contact also granted Ador rights to use the band members’ “name, photographs, likeness, handwriting, voice and any other elements” in perpetuity, in a level of ownership that goes further than government recommendations for such rights to end at the point of contract termination.

The clause also grants Ador the right to use the NewJeans members as AI chatbots or clones.

The Guardian has reached out to Hybe for comment.
