Abdul El-Sayed has won the US Senate race in Michigan, defending a Democratic seat, in one of the most closely watched competitions this midterm cycle.

El-Sayed beat former Republican congressman Mike Rogers in his bead to fill Michigan’s open Senate seat.

While El-Sayed yoked Rogers to Trump, Rogers sought to cast El-Sayed, a former public health official who ran on a platform of Medicare for All, as too extreme for Michigan.

The race was also a source of late consternation after Haley Stevens, the Democratic congresswoman who El-Sayed beat in the August primary, issued a last minute endorsement of Rogers.

Elon Musk brushed off the swathe of Republican losses in these midterm elections, by joking about his historic spending this cycle – where he spent an estimated $445m to support GOP candidates in various marquee races.

“Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” Musk posted to X. The billionaire founder of Tesla and SpaceX was the biggest donor in these elections, dwarfing any outside spending to support Democrats.

Many Democrats have vowed to investigate Musk and his work with the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (Doge), which hollowed out several federal agencies, when they take control of Congress.

The Democratic Socialists of America said that more than 50 DSA candidates won their races in tonight’s midterms.

“Workers deserve more and a reality where all of us live with dignity and hope is closer than we think,” the organization wrote in a social media post. “The job’s not done, though. Tomorrow, we continue organizing, fighting, and winning for the working class!”

Supporters of Los Angeles mayor Karen Bass appeared hopeful the incumbent could pull off a victory over challenger Nithya Raman.

Close to 11pm, a group of attendees at a LA county Democratic Party event at Loews Hollywood Hotel were dancing as they waited for more results and chanting “four more years”. Early returns showed Bass with a narrow lead in the polls.

Bass had addressed supporters earlier in the evening, praising what she described as a critical day for the city and the country as Democrats saw huge wins across the US.

“Our country has spoken. The city is speaking,” Bass said. “Let me just say from the bottom of my heart, thank you Angelenos.”

Bass faced a tough fight for re-election given her low approval ratings and Angelenos’ broad dissatisfaction with the state of the city. While her opponent Raman, an LA city councilor and one time ally, was leading the polls for weeks, Bass made gains in recent weeks.

Democrat Melissa Gonzalo said people were feeling ecstatic about the blue wave across the US, and “cautiously optimistic” about the mayor’s race. “This is a very unique situation,” she said.

As an LA county resident she can’t vote for Bass, but has convinced friends to back the mayor. Bass cares about the city and has rectified past errors, Gonzalo said.

“I don’t feel like it’s time for someone new at this moment,” she said, particularly with the upcoming Olympics.

Kevin Garrity, another Bass supporter, was hopeful given Bass’s momentum in recent weeks.

“It’s too close to call, but if I were betting on it I would vote on Karen. She’s the best candidate. She has experience. She loves this city.”

Democrat Denise Powell has won the House race for Nebraska’s second congressional district, flipping the open seat after moderate Republican incumbent – Don Bacon – announced that he would retire.

Powell beat Republican Brinker Harding in the contest, which includes Omaha – the “blue dot” of the state. The district is only one in Nebraska that Kamala Harris won in 2024.

Donald Trump answered a phone call from Politico anchor Dasha Burns on air tonight, telling the outlet that he is open to working with Democrats.

“We’re going to work with the Democrats to make sure things go well for our country,” he said, adding “I’ve already spoken to certain leaders of the Democrat party.”

“If I think it’s not good, I’m just going to veto it,” Trump added.

Democrat Katy Padilla Stout has flipped Texas’ 23rd congressional district, beating Republican Brandon Hererra for the open seat.

Turmoil beset the race after the GOP incumbent Tony Gonzales withdrew from the race amid allegations of sexual misconduct and an investigation by the House ethics committee.

Democrats are continuing to react with enthusiasm to tonight’s election results.

“Tonight, the American people sent a clear message — they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face,” former president Barack Obama wrote in a social media post. “While this administration has another two years in office, our job now is to roll up our sleeves, make changes wherever we have the power to do so, prevent further damage, and lay the groundwork for the future.”

“The American people just impeached Donald Trump,” senator Mark Kelly of Arizona wrote in a social media post.

“They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” Massachusetts senator Ed Markey wrote in a social media post replying to a comment about tech company executives. In a later post he wrote, “WHO WANTS MEDICARE FOR ALL?”

Jamie Raskin, the congressman from Maryland, quoted Tom Paine, writing in a social media post: “Tyranny, like hell, is not easily conquered, but we have this consolation: The more difficult the struggle, the more glorious in the end will be our victory.”

“A great night for the rule of law. A great night for democracy. America is back,” Minnesota governor Tim Walz wrote in a social media post.

Oregon’s Democratic governor, Tina Kotek, declared victory in a speech to supporters in Portland late Tuesday, although the race has not yet been called by the Associated Press, and her Republican challenger, Christine Drazan, refused to concede with close to a third of the votes still to be counted.

“I am proud to stand here as your next governor of the beautiful state of Oregon,” Kotek told supporters in downtown Portland after two other media outlets (CBS News and Decision Desk) projected that she would win re-election. She led 52.3%-45% at the time.

“Tina Kotek, as I’ve heard, has gone on stage and declared victory. Now all the votes haven’t been counted and I am continuing to pray for the victory for us,” Drazan said about 30 minutes later in Hillsboro, Oregon. “This race isn’t over.”

More than 100 Democratic women have been elected to the House of Representatives, marking a 60% increase in their representation since 2016.

“Women have borne the brunt of the Trump administration’s recklessness and Republicans’ extremist agenda, and on Tuesday they made it clear they have had enough, senator Teresa Leger Fernández, the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said in a statement.

“The millions of women who showed up at the polls voted for a better future for all women and girls. Their rights to healthcare, childcare, and even their right to vote was on the line,” she added.

articles.title: Miliband criticises Blair’s slavery statement and defends Burnham’s plan for proper apology – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
The foreign secretary added that the UK will not shift its position on reparations

Good morning. Wednesdays are normally the most exciting day of the week at Westminster, because it’s PMQs, but today...
articles.body_text:
The foreign secretary added that the UK will not shift its position on reparations

Good morning. Wednesdays are normally the most exciting day of the week at Westminster, because it’s PMQs, but today (unless we get some mega surprise) all the action is taking place somewhere else. In part, that’s because Andy Burnham is still at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua. But mostly because anyone in SW1 with even a passing interest in politics will be far more interested in the outcome of the US midterm elections. You can catch up with all the drama on our US politics live blog.

While the US results are undoubtedly fascinating, quite how relevant they are to the UK is a bit harder to discern. Donald Trump is still president for the next two years, and none of the chaos he has caused for Britain and other European allies is going to go away; conceivably, he could end up even more disruptive. Trump was first elected president in 2016 only months after the UK voted for Brexit and there will be progressives in Britain hoping the US results show that what Ed Davey is this morning calling the “politics of hate, division and economic harm” might be on their way out this side of the pond too. Maybe? But it is probably too soon to get carried away. Our US coverage is all here. In so far as there is any interesting UK reaction, I will post it here.

Back to the Commonwealth summit, and Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has given an interview to the BBC in which he defended Burnham’s decision to open talks about a proper UK apology for slavery. In particular, Miliband was critical of Tony Blair’s attempts to settle this issue with what Miliband described as a “sorry not sorry” apology.

Miliband was referring to this statement that Blair issued in 2006, written up at the time by the Guardian here. Blair said the slave trade was “profoundly shameful” and he expressed “deep sorrow that it ever happened”. But he did not formally apologise.

In an interview with the BBC’s Newscast podcast, Miliband said Burnham wanted a different approach. He said:

double quotation markPeople have been honestly a bit bruised by the past, what happened in the past, the sense that we just really just wanted to sweep this issue under the carpet and not confront it.

My sense is there’s a bit of a sigh of relief that, OK … at least there’s a sense of we’ve got a shared interest now in moving the Commonwealth on.

Miliband said Blair “did sort of do a kind of ‘sorry not sorry’ situation”. He added: “He kind of expressed ‘sorrow, but’ and then said sorry, and then it was walked back by No 10.”

(Miliband has for many years had a strained relationship with the former prime minister, who was opposed to the way Miliband criticised some aspects of New Labour’s record when he was party leader between 2010 and 2015. These latest remarks are just the latest example of feuding between the two of them.)

Burnham has said he wants a “structured dialogue” with Commonwealth countries about the wording of an apology. Asked whether the government might reach the point of a formal apology by the time it hosts the G20 leaders’ summit in Manchester next November, Miliband said: “Broadly speaking, yes.”

But he also stressed that the UK was not offering reparations. Asked whether the government’s new approach could end up costing UK taxpayers a penny more, Miliband replied:

double quotation markNo … For us, that’s never been what it’s about. And that’s why it’s been important that … I did have this conversation with our partners in advance. I said, ‘Look, we are going to say we are willing to say that we’re open to an apology, but we’re not going to shift our position on reparations.’

It’s not for us. It’s not the right answer. It’s not practical. It’s not feasible for us, but there are things we can work on co-operatively.

9.30am: Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, gives evidence to the Commons health committee.

10am: Lucy Powell, the education secretary, gives evidence to the Commons education committee.

Noon: Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, faces Alex Burghart, the deputy Conservative leader, at PMQs.

Afternoon (UK time): Andy Burnham is due to record a pooled TV interview while attending the final day of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda.

2.15pm: Jonathan Haskel, chair of the Office for Budget Responsibility, gives evidence with colleagues to the Commons Treasury committee about the budget.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

It is not good to gloat – but it can be fun. Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland secretary, has this morning reposted a video clip of Nigel Farage saying “I don’t go with the consensus that Trump is going to get smashed.” Bryant added: “Just leaving this here.”

Here is some reaction to the US midterm election results from British politicians. Progressives – people from Labour, the Lib Dems and the Greens – are delighted. Rightwingers seem to be largely silent about the results on social media so far. Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader who used to boast regularly about his friendship with Donald Trump, last posted on X about 12 hours ago – about migrants.

double quotation markFor anyone who believes in decency, respect and the rule of law, it feels good to see the American people so comprehensively reject Donald Trump’s politics of hate, division and economic harm.

From the Green party leader Zack Polanski

double quotation markCongratulations Abdul El-Sayed. Congratulations to everyone celebrating victories across the United States.

These are victories for communities standing up to billionaires & the media empires they own.

Around the world, we’ve all got a lot of work to do. Let’s go! ✊🏽

From Simon Hoare, a Conservative MP and chair of the Commons public administration and constitutional affairs committee

double quotation markWaking up to some incredible results from US Midterms. A massive and welcome rebuttal of Trump and Trumpism. Heaven knows how he will respond but it’s one hell of a message the American people have sent him. The decent civilised rest of the world will be glad and relieved

From Sayeeda Warsi, a former Conservative party chair who now sits as a non-affiliated peer

double quotation markHope won over hate in the US American voters in large numbers rejected the politics of bigotry and division Those that engaged in maligning, stereotyping lying and subjecting opponents to deeply personal attacks lost Let that be a lesson for those who mimic this form of politics in the UK

From the Lib Dem foreign affairs spokesperson Calum Miller

double quotation markVoters punished Trump for crashing the US economy by launching the Iran war and imposing tariffs.

British voters will not forget that Trump’s cheerleaders, Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage, wanted the UK to back him in Iran

double quotation markTrump fanboy Farage should learn from the US results that Reform’s isolationism, dodgy billionaire obsessions and divisive policies would be as damaging to UK families here as that of the man whose boots he has so often licked.

From John McDonnell, a Labour MP and former shadow chancellor

double quotation markThe US results should give confidence to progressives everywhere. People have rejected the racism displayed by Trump and his supporters and in many states have cited his brutal treatment of migrants as a factor in their decision to reject the politics of Trump.

From the Lib Dem international development spokesperson Monica Harding

double quotation markCongratulations to @RepSusieLee reelected in Nevada - I spent time on her campaign in the summer - when today’s Democrat tsunami wasn’t yet clear…. Such an exciting day for us here in the UK who are willing on all those who want to put an end to Trump’s division, corruption and economic harm that hurts us all. 🇺🇸🇬🇧

From Darren Jones, the Labour chief secretary to the PM under Keir Starmer

double quotation markThe brilliant election results from our sister party @TheDemocrats in the United States shows us something important about politics:

“The first light of dawn is on the horizon” - @ossoff

From the Labour MP for Falkirk Euan Stainbank

double quotation markThe news this morning is the best thing to come out of the US this year other than Jacob Murrell.

The Labour MP Lizzi Collinge has posted a giff implying she is pretty delighted too.

Energy bosses in the UK will have their bonuses curtailed when suppliers and brokers break the rules under a crackdown on mis-selling, Pippa Neill reports.

Andy Burnham has described the Commonwealth as “more important today than ever before” amid “such volatile times”. He used the phrase in a meeting with his Antigua and Barbuda counterpart Gaston Browne, who is hosting the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm).

In a readout of the meeting, released this morning, a No 10 spokesperson said:

double quotation markThe prime minister thanked Prime Minister Browne for the warm welcome from Antigua and Barbuda and for hosting Commonwealth leaders at such an important time.

In such volatile times, it was clear that the Commonwealth was more important today than ever before, the prime minister added.

articles.title: US contractor gave Ethiopia secrets to help kill Tigray fighters
articles.excerpt:
The devastating two-year civil war killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions

An Ethiopian-born American citizen has pleaded guilty to passing highly classified intelligence to Eth...
articles.body_text:
The devastating two-year civil war killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions

An Ethiopian-born American citizen has pleaded guilty to passing highly classified intelligence to Ethiopia, including information he hoped would help target and kill fighters from the Tigray region during the country's 2020-22 civil war.

Abraham Teklu Lemma, a former US contractor, admitted sharing dozens of classified documents and photographs with senior Ethiopian officials over more than two years, the US Department of Justice said.

"In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security," said US Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

The 54-year-old faces up to 22 years in prison under a plea agreement.

Abraham had worked as a contractor at the State Department, Justice Department and National Reconnaissance Office, the agency responsible for US intelligence satellites.

Prosecutors said Abraham worked with senior figures in Ethiopia's political, military and intelligence establishments between 2021 and his arrest in August 2023.

He secretly removed classified material from secure government facilities, sometimes copying sensitive information into handwritten notes that he carried out of the buildings. He used his position as an IT administrator to extract electronic intelligence files.

"Much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia," prosecutors said.

The information included satellite imagery and details of military activities, which he passed to Ethiopian officials through encrypted messages.

The FBI said Ethiopian officials subsequently used intelligence supplied by Abraham in military operations.

Prosecutors said he hoped the information would help Ethiopia's military identify and kill paramilitary fighters.

"Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree," said John Eisenberg, the US assistant attorney general for national security.

In one message to an Ethiopian official in December 2021, he wrote: "We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia," court papers showed.

Later that day, he shared further intelligence and urged the official: "Please send Dro[nes]."

The BBC has contacted the Ethiopian authorities for comment.

The revelations shed light on how sensitive American intelligence was passed to Ethiopian authorities during a devastating civil war that killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.

It was marked by widespread allegations of atrocities, including massacres, sexual violence and attacks on civilians.

A peace agreement signed in November 2022 ended the conflict, although fighting resumed in September after both sides accused each other of not respecting the terms of that deal.

How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia

Abraham was arrested in Maryland in August 2023 following an investigation into his handling of classified intelligence.

At the time, prosecutors alleged that he had removed security markings from intelligence reports and shared information with a foreign intelligence official.

In one exchange, the official asked him to continue providing assistance, to which Abraham replied: "Roger that!"

Pirro, the US attorney, said Abraham had abused his access to some of America's most sensitive intelligence.

She accused him of betraying his colleagues and country with prosecutors saying he "will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law".

Abraham pleaded guilty to conspiring to transmit national defence information to a foreign government.

His sentencing is scheduled for 14 April 2027.

articles.title: EU to lead talks on support for Ukraine with US, Nato, partners – Europe live
articles.excerpt:
European Commission will hold talks with the US, France, Germany, Britain, Nato, and the World Bank

With most eyes still on the US this morning, Brussels is quietly getting on with the task of leadin...
articles.body_text:
European Commission will hold talks with the US, France, Germany, Britain, Nato, and the World Bank

With most eyes still on the US this morning, Brussels is quietly getting on with the task of leading on discussions about the next round of support for Ukraine.

The European Commission will hold talks with the US, France, Germany, Britain, Nato, and the World Bank, looking what can be done to help Kyiv throughout the winter and how to support the US-led peace process with the upcoming negotiations in Abu Dhabi.

Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff said US negotiators would meet with their European partners in Brussels.

Their talks come after another night of heavy attacks on Ukraine, hitting power stations in Kyiv and Zhytomyr and a cargo vessel at sea near Odesa.

I will also bring you any European reactions to the midterms in the US, although many politicians (while quietly amused or relieved) may choose to stay silent to not risk Donald Trump’s wrath.

It’s Wednesday, 4 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

French finance minister Roland Lescure also responded to the result in the US, discussing what the next steps of the US president, Donald Trump, could be.

“Either he decides to rise above the fray – acknowledging that changes are necessary, particularly regarding gasoline prices, which directly affect people – and, I might add, he tones down his international involvement; or he does not.“

Frankly, this is something we ‌will need to keep an eye on in the coming days.“

German defence minister Boris Pistorius has congratulated the US Democeats “from the bottom of his heart” on their win last night, Dlf reported.

Deutsche Welle’s chief political correspondent Nina-Haase-Trobridge posted a longer clip of his comments at the Berlin Security Conference, with Pistorius acknowledging a “historic victory” for the Democrats.

“So for us this means we will continue our relationship based on trust and cooperation with the administration. … And, like in the past, we will have a close working relationship with the Democrats,” he said, quoted by the journalist.

“As for what we can expect now, that remains to be seen. It depends, to some extent, on what the American president intends to do following these elections,” he said in response to a question from Politico’s Rixa Fürsen.

Meanwhile, Norwegian PM Jonas Gahr Støre told Reuters:

“This is a powerful political signal about a change of course among American voters.

Voices are ⁠now emerging in American politics that are closer to us than the president and the administration have stood for, for example on climate and environment, and in foreign policy and development aid policy.“

Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, who also clashed with Trump in recent months, wasn’t in the mood to offer any reaction to the US elections this morning, as she told reporters, via Corriere:

“We’ll talk about America some other time. Right now, it’s Armed Forces Day, 4 November.”

But opposition politicians celebrated the result, with former prime minister Matteo Renzi calling it “wonderful” and a response to Trump’s “abuse” of his position.

“Trump has another two years to go, but the Maga movement has been severely weakened, if not defeated.”

MEP Sandro Gozi said the electorate’s verdict “offers renewed hope that the next two years will mark the beginning of the end of the Trump era.”

Meanwhile, Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski ridiculed the Polish right, which has been supportive of Trump since his return to the office.

Paraphrasing Jesus’s words from the Bible (sic!), he said:

“Truly I tell you, before the rooster crows, they will disown him three times”

He also took swipe at US billionaire Elon Musk who donated hundreds of millions of dollars into Republican campaigns, reposting his comment from one of their previous clashes, saying:

“See, big man, politics is harder than you thought.”

For what it’s worth, Musk also appeared to see a funny side in his involvement in the campaign, saying:

“Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time.”

Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – who has been Donald Trump’s most vociferous European critic – is celebrating last night’s results in the US, hailing them as proof of a progressive fightback and of the “crumbling” of what he called the “ultra wave”.

“Yesterday, American society voted against the policies that only impoverish,” he posted on X. “Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites.”

Sánchez, who faces an uphill battle to secure another term in office in Spain’s general election at the end of the month, added:

“It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain.”

With most eyes still on the US this morning, Brussels is quietly getting on with the task of leading on discussions about the next round of support for Ukraine.

The European Commission will hold talks with the US, France, Germany, Britain, Nato, and the World Bank, looking what can be done to help Kyiv throughout the winter and how to support the US-led peace process with the upcoming negotiations in Abu Dhabi.

Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff said US negotiators would meet with their European partners in Brussels.

Their talks come after another night of heavy attacks on Ukraine, hitting power stations in Kyiv and Zhytomyr and a cargo vessel at sea near Odesa.

I will also bring you any European reactions to the midterms in the US, although many politicians (while quietly amused or relieved) may choose to stay silent to not risk Donald Trump’s wrath.

It’s Wednesday, 4 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.title: Babcock launches digital platform to link warship construction and fleet support
articles.excerpt:
VIENNA — U.K-based Babcock International has launched Pelorus, a digital platform intended to connect warship construction, operations and maintenance data.

The British defense and engineering compan...
articles.body_text:
VIENNA — U.K-based Babcock International has launched Pelorus, a digital platform intended to connect warship construction, operations and maintenance data.

The British defense and engineering company announced the launch Nov. 3 at the Euronaval defense trade show in Paris, saying the platform already operates in selected Babcock-managed maritime construction and support environments. Babcock did not identify the deployments or customers involved, or provide figures showing how the platform has affected fleet availability or maintenance costs.

According to the company, Pelorus combines information from multiple systems to track shipbuilding progress, commissioning and trials, fleet availability, maintenance and logistics.

“The future of maritime capability depends on the ability to connect design, production, operational and support data into a single digital environment,” said Nick Hine, Babcock’s chief growth officer and marine chief executive, in the announcement.

The company positioned the platform as supporting both existing fleets and future combinations of crewed and autonomous vessels, linking it to its ARMOR Force concept − short for Autonomous and Remote, Maritime Operational Response Force. Babcock said Pelorus could also be adapted for other defense and critical infrastructure applications.

Babcock’s naval business spans shipbuilding and long-term fleet support. The company is building five Type 31 frigates for Britain’s Royal Navy at its Rosyth yard in Scotland. It also maintains and upgrades British nuclear-powered submarines at Devonport and Clyde, according to its website.

articles.title: US midterm elections 2026: live results from Senate, House and governor races in all 50 states
articles.excerpt:
With many seats still to come in, the Democrats have taken control of the Senate, House and several key governorships. Find live updating results in full here

Most US election seats are reliably won ...
articles.body_text:
With many seats still to come in, the Democrats have taken control of the Senate, House and several key governorships. Find live updating results in full here

Most US election seats are reliably won by one party, so control of Congress comes down to a few competitive "battleground" seats. Experts track these to predict overall results; if a party wins seats they were expected to lose, it often signals a successful night. In the charts below, blue shapes on the right signal a good night for the Democrats, and red shapes on the left signal that the Republicans have done well.

Before the election, the Cook Report classified six Senate races as genuine "toss-ups". The Democrats need to win at least three of these, alongside the other races they are expected to win.

Democrats were favoured in enough House seats to take the chamber without winning any of the 18 seats the Cook Political Report classed as “toss-ups”. If they won every seat they were expected to win, they would comfortably win a majority. The balance of power rested on whether Democrats would hold the 18 seats rated “lean Democratic”. Republicans, favoured in 195 seats, would have needed to sweep all 18 toss-ups and flip five Democratic-leaning seats to win.

Thirty-three of the 100 members of the upper chamber were being elected regularly this year, along with two other special elections. Republicans had the Senate majority before the election. Senators serve six-year terms.

Republicans were defending a majority in the 435-member House. Democrats held 212 House seats and needed 218 to win control. Members of the House of Representatives serve two-year terms and face re-election every even year.

Gubernatorial elections were taking place in 36 states, as well as three territories. Republicans and Democrats held 18 of these state governorships each before the election. Three incumbent governors were retiring.

The US legislature, Congress, has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate.

How is the House of Representatives elected and how do they work?

The lower chamber, the House of Representatives, has 435 voting seats, each representing a district of roughly similar size. There are elections for each of these seats every two years.

The speaker of the House is the chamber’s presiding officer, elected by the representatives. The House has several exclusive powers, such as the power to initiate revenue bills, impeach federal officials and elect the president in the case of an electoral college tie.

How is the Senate elected and how do they work?

The upper chamber, the Senate, has 100 members, who sit for six-year terms. One-third of the seats come up for election in each two-year cycle. Each state has two senators, regardless of its population; this means that Wyoming, with a population of less than 600,000, carries the same weight as California, with almost 40 million.

Most legislation needs to pass both chambers to become law, but the Senate has some important other functions, notably approving senior presidential appointments, for instance to the supreme court. The Senate also has the sole power to provide advice to the president, consent to ratify treaties and try impeachment cases for federal officials referred to it by the House.

In most states, the candidate with the most votes on election day wins the seat. However, Georgia and Louisiana require the winning candidate to garner 50% of votes cast; if no one does, they hold a runoff election between the top two candidates.

Maine and Alaska use ranked-choice voting as opposed to the first past the post voting system in congressional elections. Voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives a majority of first-choice votes, the least-supported candidate is eliminated and their ballots are transferred to each voter’s next-ranked candidate. This continues until a candidate wins a majority.

In some states, an election can feature two candidates from the same party. Under top-two or “jungle” primary systems, candidates from all parties compete in the same primary and the two receiving the most votes advance, regardless of party. The congressional election candidates could both be Democrats or both be Republicans.

Florida and Ohio are having ‘special elections’ for the Senate because the previous holders of their seats – Marco Rubio and JD Vance – resigned to join the executive branch following the 2024 presidential election.

How are governors elected and how do they work?

Governors are elected by direct vote in their states. The candidate with the highest number of votes is declared the winner.

In every state, the executive branch is led by a governor. They serve for four years in office, with the exception of Vermont and New Hampshire where tenures are two years long.

Governors are responsible for implementing state laws, and have a range of powers available to them such as executive orders, executive budgets and legislative proposals and vetoes.

The election results on this page are reported by the Associated Press. AP will “call” the winner in a state when it determines that the trailing candidate has no path to victory. This can happen before 100% of votes in a state have been counted.

Estimates for the total vote in each state are also provided by AP. The numbers update throughout election night and in the following days, as more data on voter turnout becomes available.

Antonio Voce, Seán Clarke, Ed Gargan, Anna Leach and Ashley Kirk

articles.title: Rwanda's army team removed from Africa league after US sanctions, NBA says
articles.excerpt:
Rwanda's army team APR came third in the Basketball Africa League last year

The National Basketball Association (NBA) says it removed Rwanda's army team from its African league because of US sanction...
articles.body_text:
Rwanda's army team APR came third in the Basketball Africa League last year

The National Basketball Association (NBA) says it removed Rwanda's army team from its African league because of US sanctions imposed on the country in March.

The NBA had previously said the Rwandan army-funded Armée Patriotique Rwandaise (APR) club would not participate in the 2026 Basketball Africa League (BAL).

However this is the first time the NBA has revealed the reasons behind the APR's removal.

The association was responding to complaints by two US senators, who sent a letter asking them to reconsider their partnership with the Rwandan team. The US placed sanctions on the Rwandan army, accusing it of fuelling the conflict in the Democratic Republic of Congo in March.

The senators said the NBA risked "becoming complicit in sportswashing by accepting money from a Rwandan government that systematically abuses human rights".

Last week, the US also imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry over its support for the M23 rebel group which has seized control of large parts of eastern DR Congo. Rwanda denies backing the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.

Rwanda is an official BAL partner and pays the league to host its finals at the 10,000-seat BK Arena in the capital, Kigali.

The evidence that shows Rwanda is backing rebels in DR Congo

In the letter to the NBA dated 23 October, Democratic Senator Jeffrey Merkley and Republican counterpart Marsha Blackburn gave the association until 2 November to give a written response regarding its continued partnership with Rwanda.

"What is the NBA red line for accepting money from foreign governments that commit human rights abuses?" the senators asked.

Among other queries, they also questioned how the association could "reconcile its continued partnership with Rwanda with its purported commitment to justice".

In its response, NBA deputy commissioner Mark Tatum said the Rwandan team "had been withdrawn" from the BAL following the sanctions imposed earlier in the year, American sports website ESPN reports.

The BAL is a pan-African basketball league established and co-organised by the NBA and the basketball's world governing body Fiba.

The NBA said the APR basketball club would remain barred while the US sanctions are in place.

The APR is one of Rwanda's top basketball teams and represented the country in the African league in 2024 and 2025, when it came third. It was replaced by the RSSB Tigers this year.

Rwanda has hosted all but one of the league's final and playoff matches since the inaugural match in 2021.

The NBA reportedly receives millions of dollars annually from the country for the marketing and partnership rights.

DR Congo has repeatedly condemned Rwanda's high-profile international sports deals, including with the NBA, European football clubs and Formula 1, asking them to end their campaigns.

It argues that these help Rwanda clean up its global image, while the conflict continues in eastern DR Congo.
