articles.title: Studios destroyed, traditions saved: Artists fight to save Sudan’s culture
articles.excerpt:
Port Sudan, Sudan – Awad Haroun, 45, a visual artist and theatre director, fled his home in Al-Halfaya, Khartoum North, after war destroyed a life he had worked hard to build in the capital.

He moved...
articles.body_text:
Port Sudan, Sudan – Awad Haroun, 45, a visual artist and theatre director, fled his home in Al-Halfaya, Khartoum North, after war destroyed a life he had worked hard to build in the capital.

He moved to Port Sudan with his wife and son, leaving behind his home, artistic workspace and the tools he needed to work, shortly after fighting erupted between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary in April 2023.

When he fled, he carried little: Two shirts, two pairs of trousers, two books and a few torn drawing papers, expecting to return soon. Instead, he has been forced to rebuild his life far from home.

He lost not only his home but also the tools and materials he relied on to work and make a living.

In Port Sudan, he looked to use his skills in sculpture, design and decoration for some money. He has since participated in theatrical performances at Wasel Festival, organised by Ahalina Cultural Group in partnership with UNESCO, and led traditional arts workshops with cultural groups.

Awad founded Ahalina cultural group in 2013 with a group of young people, using theatre, visual arts, music and puppetry to engage with young people and promote peace and social cohesion.

Drawing, storytelling, music and play have also given children opportunities to express themselves and connect with others.

“Losing my tools does not mean I have lost my skills, and losing my workspace does not mean I have lost my ability to create,” Awad told Al Jazeera.

Awad and other displaced artists found shelter at an old school in Port Sudan, where they helped clean and prepare the building for families forced from their homes.

“Now, concerns about the possibility of eviction have left us uncertain about where we will go next,” he said.

While art cannot replace a lost home or end the war, Awad believes it can preserve memories, bring communities together and offer children space to play and express themselves.

“From the ashes, we will rise” is the motto of Ahalina cultural group. This is more than a slogan for Awad; it is a reminder to keep creating, despite everything the war has taken from him.

The war has taken a heavy toll on Sudan’s cultural life, damaging heritage sites and disrupting the livelihoods of artists across the country.

In June 2026, UNESCO estimated that Sudan’s cultural sector faced a $30m funding gap. But behind this figure are deeply personal losses: Artists killed by the war or forced to leave behind studios, galleries, artworks and the tools they need to create.

In April 2024, UNESCO reported that the Artists and Writers Union in Port Sudan had provided shelter to more than 112 displaced artists and other cultural professionals.

The challenges remain significant, but cultural initiatives have continued. In April 2026, UNESCO said its initiatives in Port Sudan had benefitted more than 350 artists, women, girls and internally displaced cultural professionals, supporting efforts to sustain Sudan’s cultural life amid the conflict.

Asim Abdelaziz, 31, a musician and filmmaker, left El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, amid escalating fighting and repeated drone attacks. He arrived in Port Sudan in November 2023, hoping to find safety and work.

Separated from his family, who are scattered between Omdurman and El Obeid, Asim lives alone in a shelter for displaced artists. The war has uprooted his life and disrupted his career, but he continues to use music to preserve Sudan’s cultural heritage and bring communities together.

In Port Sudan, he has worked with the local Artists and Writers Union, UNESCO and community organisations.  He has also collaborated with the Ministry of Culture and Information and other artists on music programmes to address social issues, including hate speech and racism.

Asim said the war has spurred hate speech and deepened divisions between Sudan’s different communities. He believes art can counter these differences by promoting diversity, mutual acceptance and peaceful coexistence.

“I have seen firsthand how hate speech affects people’s lives,” Asim told Al Jazeera. “Through music, I try to remind Sudanese people that we are all brothers and sisters, and that war does not represent who we are.”

Mokhalaya, a project he founded to document and archive traditional music and rhythms from across the country a year ago, is one avenue for this.

“I hope to take the project to international festivals, introducing audiences abroad to [showcase] Sudan’s rich musical traditions and cultural diversity,” he said.

Preserving heritage is not just about safeguarding the past, but also about keeping Sudan’s cultural identity alive during a war that has displaced communities and disrupted lives, he said.

Abdelqader Hashem, secretary of the Red Sea State Writers and Artists Union, told Al Jazeera the union has supported artists and their families who fled fighting in other parts of Sudan since the war began on April 15, 2023.

“We worked to establish a shelter for displaced artists in a school in Port Sudan and sought support from local and international organisations to provide for their basic needs,” he said.

Beyond providing shelter, the union has helped displaced artists take part in the city’s cultural activities, contributing to community awareness programmes that address important societal issues such as the dangers of drug use, a growing concern in Sudan.

“We have also implemented projects in partnership with UNESCO to train children in displacement camps in handicrafts, including concrete crafts,” Hashem said.

“Most of the displaced artists have since returned to their homes in Khartoum following the Sudanese army’s recapture of the capital.”

articles.title: Alaska’s two ‘Dan Sullivans’: How common is ballot stacking, does it work?
articles.excerpt: The Alaska Senate ballot in the next week’s midterm elections in the United States features two candidates with the name Dan Sullivan – one the incumbent Republican senator and another a retired teach...
articles.body_text:
The Alaska Senate ballot in the next week’s midterm elections in the United States features two candidates with the name Dan Sullivan – one the incumbent Republican senator and another a retired teacher with no prior political experience.

Last week, The New York Times reported that aides to Mary Peltola, the Alaska Democrat challenging Republican Senator Sullivan for a crucial seat, helped recruit candidates bearing names similar to Sullivan’s in an apparent bid to manipulate the ballot and siphon votes from the incumbent.

The controversy has triggered a political firestorm in the US, and prompted President Donald Trump to order a Justice Department investigation into alleged voter fraud.

“It was a scheme. It was election fraud. Total election fraud,” Trump said. Peltola has rejected the accusations, saying the dispute is distracting from voters’ concerns.

On Friday, US Attorney Michael Heyman said Democrats had “orchestrated a sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up Daniel J Sullivan as a sham candidate”, adding that “we are taking that extremely seriously”.

So, how common is this electoral tactic – and does it work? We look at history to find out.

Daniel J Sullivan Jr, the second Dan Sullivan, announced his US Senate candidacy on May 29, just three days before Alaska’s June 1 filing deadline. The Republican nominee on the ballot is also called Dan Sullivan. The second Sullivan has repeatedly denied any Democratic push behind his candidacy.

However, the Times’s reporting earlier this week triggered a political storm over allegations that Democratic operatives had sought to manipulate Alaska’s crucial US Senate race by recruiting candidates to split votes for Republican incumbent Sullivan.

The report alleged that people aligned with Peltola, her campaign’s lawyers and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) had coordinated an initiative to recruit candidates who could dilute Sullivan’s support – internally called the “ballot composition project”.

According to the Times, a Peltola campaign staffer was tasked with identifying Alaskans named Dan Sullivan.

The strategy, commonly called “ballot stacking”, involves recruiting or encouraging candidates to enter a race not necessarily to win, but to influence the distribution of votes and improve another candidate’s chances.

Alaska has four candidates on the ballot – and the presence of two candidates named Sullivan could potentially confuse voters.

The report prompted Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy to order a criminal investigation.

“I just want to clear the air,” Peltola said at the top of a speech in a downtown bar in Juneau, Alaska’s capital, on Friday. “I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters.”

The race is considered key to control of the US Senate.

Past instances show that the strategy can work at times to manipulate voters.

One of the starkest examples emerged in Florida’s 2020 state Senate race, when Republican political operative and former state senator Frank Artiles allegedly orchestrated a scheme to recruit a namesake candidate to undermine Democratic incumbent Jose Javier Rodriguez.

According to prosecutors, Artiles paid Alex Rodriguez, who shared the incumbent’s surname, to enter the race as an independent candidate to confuse voters and divert ballots from the Democrat to his Republican challenger, Ileana Garcia.

Incumbent senator Jose lost by just 32 votes – while the other Rodriguez garnered more than 6,000 votes without having led a meaningful campaign.

Later, Alex Rodriguez pleaded guilty to campaign finance violations in 2021 and agreed to cooperate with investigators, and Artiles was later convicted in connection with the scheme and fined.

Similarly, in 2024, Washington’s Democratic state Attorney General Bob Ferguson was joined by two namesakes in the primary race, after a Republican activist was alleged to have paid the other two Fergusons to run.

However, Democratic leader Bob Ferguson threatened legal action – and the decoys dropped out. Ferguson was elected governor.

Though stacking a ballot is a political tactic used in other countries as well, the US has seen a couple of its own instances, in Florida and Washington.

During John F Kennedy’s first congressional campaign, a second candidate named Joseph Russo entered the Democratic primary for Massachusetts’ 11th Congressional District. The first Joseph Russo was a prominent Boston city councillor who opposed Kennedy.

Kennedy’s campaign manager and his father, Joseph P Kennedy Sr, have been implicated in accounts of the alleged scheme, but the extent of JFK’s personal involvement remains disputed.

In the June 1946 primary, Kennedy received 22,183 votes, while the two Russos collectively received 6,460. Kennedy won the nomination.

In India, the world’s most populous country, fielding such namesakes is a common tactic – but not always a successful one.

In the 2019 national election, Congress president Rahul Gandhi, the scion of the Gandhi family, faced three namesakes in Wayanad, Kerala, in southern India. The candidates were named: Rahul Gandhi K E, Raghul Gandhi K, and K M Sivaprasad Gandhi.

Congress’s Rahul Gandhi won Wayanad by a landslide, however, securing 706,367 votes.

In the 2014 national election, Bollywood actor and a candidate of the Bharatiya Janata Party, Hema Malini, faced two namesakes in Mathura, Uttar Pradesh. The actor also won that election decisively.

In the 2014 election, in Mahasamund in Chhattisgarh, Congress candidate Ajit Jogi faced BJP’s Chandu Lal Sahu in a race with seven other candidates named Chandu Lal Sahu. BJP’s Sahu won by a margin of nearly 11,000 votes, whereas his namesakes collectively got 62,934 votes.

But for some, it has proven costly in India. Also in the 2014 election, incumbent Member of Parliament, K Sudhakaran from Congress, was defeated by a margin of 6,566 votes. His two namesakes, K Sudhakaran Sreeshylam and K Sudhakaran Kollon, secured 2,745 and 4,240 votes, respectively.

articles.title: New Yemen fighting displaces 290,000, says UN, with pregnant women at risk
articles.excerpt:
At least 290,000 have been displaced in Yemen since the country’s war re-erupted in August, according to the United Nations’ humanitarian office (OCHA), with a dire threat to pregnant women.

Fighting...
articles.body_text:
At least 290,000 have been displaced in Yemen since the country’s war re-erupted in August, according to the United Nations’ humanitarian office (OCHA), with a dire threat to pregnant women.

Fighting between forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally-recognised government and Houthi rebels has intensified, particularly in Taiz governorate and coastal areas, with thousands reported killed.

An OCHA report published Friday warned that 65,000 refugees and asylum seekers in Yemen face a rapidly deteriorating situation, with services disrupted and food and fuel prices rapidly rising. Among those recently displaced are 6,100 pregnant women, including 600 due to give birth within two weeks.

The UN has sent mobile teams and midwives to displacement sites, and aid groups have been able to deliver food, hygiene supplies and emergency cash to about 249,000 people – about three in four among the displaced.

The rise in displacement comes as the war has escalated on several fronts and reached across the border into Saudi Arabia, where on Saturday the Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted and destroyed a “hostile” drone over the Riyadh region.

“The relevant authorities are continuing to inspect the site,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki wrote in a post on X, but said no casualties had been reported. It is the second interception over the Riyadh region in as many days.

On Friday, Saudi Arabia said drones had been downed near Mecca, Medina and Riyadh, along with a Houthi missile fired towards the kingdom’s south.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree denied that the group had launched drones towards Saudi territory, calling the claims “egregious lies”.

The group has repeatedly denied aiming at Islam’s two holiest cities, while claiming responsibility for attacks on the Saudi capital, airports and oil infrastructure.

The Houthis’ attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on October 10 killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300, the most lethal attack on Saudi soil in more than a decade.

Saudi Minister of Foreign Affairs Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud attended a G20 Foreign Ministers meeting in Atlanta, Georgia on Saturday, where he discussed the situation in Yemen with United States, Russian and European counterparts, according to the Saudi state news agency.

Prince Faisal and Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand also issued a joint condemnation of the Houthi attacks on the kingdom on the sidelines of the meeting.

Yemen’s internationally recognised government announced on Friday that the Houthis had fired at least three ballistic missiles at Maashiq presidential palace, the seat of government in Aden, the interim capital of Yemen.

They also fired missiles at Aden International airport, which had reopened on Thursday after a brief closure for repairs following an earlier Houthi attack.

Both the palace and the airport have been repeat targets for Houthi drone and missile attacks in recent weeks.

The cabinet of Yemen’s internationally recognised government denounced the attacks, calling the airport strike “a direct attack on the interest of citizens” and accusing the group of seeking to disrupt “legitimate institutions” by striking the palace.

Spokesman for Yemen’s government forces, Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili, said on Friday they “neutralised” about 336 Houthi fighters and commanders and destroyed or damaged 112 vehicles, weapons and other equipment “in recent hours”.

Warplanes, drones, artillery and rocket launchers targeted the group’s command centres, troop concentrations and supply routes on fronts including Taiz, Marib, al-Jawf and al-Bayda, he said.

One civilian was killed and five injured, including a child, in Houthi attacks across Taiz governorate, according to the government-aligned Saba news agency. The agency reported that a woman was shot dead, while the injuries came from shelling and gunfire.

The UN has verified 270 civilian casualties since August, including 68 killed, half of whom are children.

The Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedoms said its field team in Taiz province has recorded thousands of Houthi violations between September 1 and October 29, with at least 189 civilians killed, including 38 children and 27 women.

The group said it recorded 23 field executions and more than 300 abductions or enforced disappearances.

Roads have also been closed by the fighting, blocking food, medicine, fuel and water to two million people in the vicinity.

Taiz city has been bitterly contested throughout Yemen’s civil war. After seizing ground to its south this month, including al-Turbah, the Houthis have tightened their grip around Taiz, leading to deteriorating humanitarian conditions within the city.

Yemen’s war broke out in September 2014, when Houthi forces captured the capital Sanaa, forcing the government south. The war intensified when a Saudi-led Arab coalition intervened to support government-aligned forces in March 2015.

Following several truces between the two sides, fighting re-erupted after Yemeni government forces targeted Sanaa International airport, preventing a plane carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. Since then, the Houthis have launched a sweeping offensive on Yemen’s coast, giving them control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait. Yemen’s government has announced the launch of an offensive to retake territories from the Houthis.

articles.title: LeBron James, Tyrese Maxey shine as 76ers beat Knicks in NBA Cup thriller
articles.excerpt:
LeBron James scored 20 points, including a late tip-in, to help seal the Philadelphia 76ers’ 98-93 victory over the NBA champions New York Knicks on Friday.

The 76ers notched their second win of the ...
articles.body_text:
LeBron James scored 20 points, including a late tip-in, to help seal the Philadelphia 76ers’ 98-93 victory over the NBA champions New York Knicks on Friday.

The 76ers notched their second win of the young season over the Knicks after spoiling their championship banner-raising with a victory at Madison Square Garden on opening night.

The win had a double edge as Friday’s games marked the start of the fourth edition of the NBA Cup, the NBA in-season tournament won by the Knicks before they went on to beat the San Antonio Spurs in the NBA Finals for their first championship since 1973.

Group-stage Cup games will be played throughout November, all counting in the regular-season standings. Quarterfinals will be played December 4-5 and semifinals December 8-9 before the final on December 11 at Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Indiana.

Tyrese Maxey scored 27 points to lead the Sixers, who took control early against the sloppy Knicks.

They led by 14 in the third quarter and weathered a late Knicks surge.

Jalen Brunson’s step-back three-pointer put New York up 90-89 with 1:32 remaining.

James, the NBA’s all-time leading scorer, answered with a basket that put Philadelphia back in front and pushed the lead to 96-91 with a tip-in off a Maxey miss with 11.9 seconds left.

James, 41, added nine rebounds, eight assists, one steal and a vintage chase-down block in what 76ers coach Nick Nurse called his best game since joining as a free agent in July.

“I thought he was really good all the way through,” Nurse said. “When we got some downhill stuff, he used his size and knocked them around a little bit for some layups … kind of pushed and organised it.

“He’s been good, but that was his best game, for sure.”

Brunson led New York with 24 points, and Karl-Anthony Towns added 22 points and 12 rebounds for the Knicks, who fell to 2-4.

The Dallas Mavericks, fuelled by 35 points from Kyrie Irving and 33 from Cooper Flagg, rallied to hand the Houston Rockets their first defeat of the season, 116-111.

The Rockets had emerged from a back-and-forth first half with a 51-44 lead, pushing the advantage to as many as 11 before taking an eight-point lead into the final frame.

Irving’s three-pointer with 7:01 remaining put Dallas back in front, and they wouldn’t trail again, the Mavs finding an answer when Houston twice pulled level in the final stretch.

“It felt good,” Irving said. “We came in at halftime, we weren’t proud of our effort. We looked each other in the eye, and we were just like, we’ve got to do better.

“We didn’t bring it in the first half, but the second half we definitely brought it.”

Golden State star Stephen Curry scored 31 points to lead the Warriors to a 112-95 victory over the Los Angeles Lakers in a rollercoaster contest in San Francisco.

The Lakers outscored the Warriors 38-15 in the first quarter, the Warriors erasing the 23-point deficit by outscoring Los Angeles 38-15 in the second to knot it 53-53 at halftime.

Luka Doncic scored 37 points for the Lakers. The night’s abiding image was of him crashing to the floor as he was wrong-footed by Curry – who fired over him for a three-pointer.

Curry took his career points tally to 26,674, surpassing Dominique Wilkins (26,668) for 18th on the all-time scoring list.

In Miami, Giannis Antetokounmpo delivered a triple-double of 31 points, 18 rebounds and 10 assists to propel the Heat to a 145-125 victory over the Indiana Pacers.

In Boston, the Celtics romped to a 125-111 victory over the Chicago Bulls. Payton Pritchard scored 30 points off the bench, and Jayson Tatum scored 26 for the Celtics, who led by as many as 32 points.

Orlando’s Desmond Bane scored 28 points, Franz Wagner added 26 and Wendell Carter chipped in 20 as the Magic fended off a late challenge to beat the Raptors 121-114 in Toronto.

The Magic drained 18 three-pointers and withstood a career-high 41-point performance from Toronto’s Scottie Barnes.

Detroit shook off a slow start to hand the winless Nets a fifth straight defeat in Brooklyn, where Cade Cunningham scored 20 points, and Ron Holland added 18 off the bench in a 110-94 Pistons victory.

articles.title: The selective solidarity at the heart of India’s voter protests
articles.excerpt: Across India, opposition parties, students and farmers are protesting against a sweeping revision of electoral rolls that has removed some 130 million names. They are demanding the restoration of the ...
articles.body_text:
Across India, opposition parties, students and farmers are protesting against a sweeping revision of electoral rolls that has removed some 130 million names. They are demanding the restoration of the old voter lists and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar. The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) – as the Election Commission of India (ECI) calls the exercise – requires voters to prove their eligibility, often through old documents.

Six years ago, Muslims took to the streets to warn that making citizenship dependent on such paperwork could leave millions vulnerable to exclusion, particularly Muslims. Their warnings were largely ignored. Now that the threat of exclusion extends beyond Muslims, many who ignored their warnings are taking to the streets themselves.

I am proud to see common people across India taking risks for one another in these protests. But I cannot ignore the hypocrisy in the opposition’s response: while it is right to challenge the SIR, its demands leave untouched the citizenship law against which Muslims protested in 2019 and the suspicion cast on them as “infiltrators”.

Some of those now marching against the revision once opposed the 2019 protests themselves. The question is whether this movement will challenge the discrimination Muslims warned about, or simply demand protection for those now caught in the same machinery.

In December 2019, Parliament passed the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), which fast-tracks citizenship for persecuted members of six religious communities from three Muslim-majority neighbours. Islam is the one major faith of the region it leaves out.

The danger lay in what the government planned to pair it with. That April, Amit Shah, now India’s home minister, told reporters in Kolkata, the capital of the eastern state of West Bengal, to “understand the chronology”: the citizenship bill first, a National Register of Citizens (NRC) after it. The NRC would be a nationwide register of Indian citizens, requiring people to prove their citizenship to be included. In November 2019, he told Parliament that the NRC would be carried out across the country.

Muslims understood the sequence at once. Anyone unable to prove their citizenship risked being excluded from the register. How could people who could barely afford shelter or two meals a day be expected to produce old documents they had never been required to keep? The CAA would then offer a way back to everyone it caught, except Muslims.

Muslim women staged a sit-in at Shaheen Bagh in the national capital territory of Delhi that continued through the winter. They were not simply warning about a future NRC, but refusing to accept a citizenship law that discriminated on religious grounds. On December 22, Prime Minister Narendra Modi insisted that his government had never discussed a nationwide NRC. Much of the country took him at his word.

Six years later, documents are being demanded anyway by a different office and under a different name. When the ECI ordered the revision in the state of Bihar on June 24, 2025, it listed the “inclusion of the names of foreign illegal immigrants” among its reasons. Its document rules turned on two birth dates, July 1, 1987 and December 2, 2004. The later you were born, the more of your parents’ documents you had to produce. In the Supreme Court, the ECI’s lawyer said the revision verifies citizenship according to the 2003 amendment. This means that a voter list is, in effect, being used as a register of citizens, without the government ever announcing an NRC.

In Parliament last December, Amit Shah said the SIR was meant to “detect, delete and deport infiltrators”. He has separated refugees from infiltrators by motive. In his account, refugees come seeking safety for their religion, while infiltrators cross for economic reasons. That is the distinction the CAA writes into law. In Indian politics, the word ghuspaithiya, which means infiltrator in Hindi, has a well-understood target. In West Bengal, Suvendu Adhikari, the BJP leader who now governs the state, promised that the SIR would “strike out the Bangladeshi Muslims from the electoral rolls”. The ECI has still not revealed how many foreigners it found.

West Bengal is where the revision has run its full course, so it is where we can see what it does. About 9.1 million names, roughly 12 percent of the electorate, were removed before the state voted in April. By one booth-level count, almost two-thirds of those removed were Hindus. Most were dropped at the first stage, where officers mark voters as absent, shifted, dead or duplicated. At that stage, Hindus and Muslims were removed roughly in proportion to their numbers.

The second stage is where the state had to make judgements. About six million voters whose forms showed what the ECI called “logical discrepancies” were sent to judicial officers. A discrepancy could be as small as a parent’s name spelt one way in the 2002 roll and another way now. The judicial officers removed 2.7 million people. Of those removed at this second stage, about 70 percent were identified as Muslim by surname in an analysis of the ECI’s published lists. Muslims make up about a quarter of the state’s electorate. Researchers at the Sabar Institute in Kolkata found that Muslims had, if anything, been more successful at tracing their families to the old rolls and were more likely to have been at home when officers visited. They were removed at the stage where the outcome turned on an official’s discretion.

In October last year, as the revision reached West Bengal, the state BJP planned about 700 camps in border districts to help Hindu refugees apply for citizenship under the CAA. The message was that those who applied would keep their place on the roll. A Hindu refugee family struck off in West Bengal has a statute written for it, but a Muslim family missing the same paper has a tribunal whose backlog could take years to clear.

The exclusions extend beyond West Bengal. In Delhi, the draft roll published on August 31 left out 4.75 million of the city’s 14.5 million voters. Okhla, the Delhi Legislative Assembly constituency that includes Shaheen Bagh and Jamia Nagar, lost 45 percent of its electorate. Patel Nagar, a seat reserved for Dalit candidates, lost 42 percent.

The fact that voters beyond the Muslim community are now struggling to prove they belong on the electoral roll should strengthen the demand for safeguards. But who exactly are those safeguards meant to protect?

The movement’s own words are the best evidence. On September 30, the opposition bloc of the Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance (INDIA) set out its “non-negotiable” demands. Those were CEC Kumar’s removal, the pre-SIR rolls, paper ballots, an appeals mechanism and “protection for genuine voters from exclusion due to technical/administrative reasons”.

The problem I see with that last phrase is that it protects the genuine voter from a careless official. It has nothing to say about the voter whom the state has decided is not genuine, and in West Bengal that voter was most often Muslim. This month, Shah accused the opposition of planning to register infiltrators as voters. The Congress party replied by asking how many infiltrators the SIR had actually caught, and whether infiltration had grown on his watch. It was meant as a rebuke. It also accepted his premise.

Some of the people now leading these marches held that premise long before the SIR existed. On October 4, cousins Uddhav Thackeray and Raj Thackeray led protests in Mumbai, the capital of the western state of Maharashtra, demanding that the revision be scrapped. In February 2020, Raj’s Maharashtra Navnirman Sena party marched through Mumbai to Azad Maidan. It demanded the eviction of Pakistani and Bangladeshi “infiltrators”, and Raj called it a “befitting reply” to the anti-CAA protests. He told the crowd he did not understand why Muslims were protesting against the CAA and the NRC.

The test of solidarity, then, is whether people will defend the rights of those whose political claims are considered inconvenient, too communal or too risky to repeat in public.

That is also why the question of those imprisoned after the anti-CAA protests cannot be separated from the current mobilisation. Activists Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam remain in prison in the larger conspiracy case connected to the 2020 Delhi violence. Their cases are not a substitute for the concerns of millions facing electoral-roll exclusions. Their continued imprisonment is another test of whether the present movement is prepared to stand with those who protested against the CAA in 2019.

If this movement wants to show it has learned anything from 2019, it needs to challenge the CAA and demand the release of those still held in the Delhi “larger conspiracy” case. If it stops at the old rolls and paper ballots, it will have defended those threatened by the SIR while leaving the discriminatory citizenship law that Muslims protested against six years ago untouched.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Storm warnings for Melbourne, Canberra, Sydney and Brisbane as cold front ‘packs a punch’
articles.excerpt:
BoM predicts hail, damaging winds and possible flash flooding across Victoria, NSW and parts of Queensland into Sunday

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Storm warnings are ...
articles.body_text:
BoM predicts hail, damaging winds and possible flash flooding across Victoria, NSW and parts of Queensland into Sunday

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Storm warnings are in place for multiple capital cities across Australia’s east and south-east as a severe weather front sweeps across the country.

Heavy rain, winds and thunderstorms are forecast to hit Melbourne and eastern Victoria throughout Saturday afternoon as a cold front meets warm, humid air.

The storm front is then expected to travel further east, impacting Canberra and inland NSW before reaching the east coast on Sunday, stretching as far as southern Queensland.

The Bureau of Meteorology warned of possible flash flooding in some areas and potentially destructive winds of over 125km/h that could bring down large trees or damage property.

Melbourne and parts of Victoria recorded moderate rainfall and some lightning on Saturday morning, with a more intense band of thunderstorms forecast into the afternoon.

“It’s this follow-up band of storms which could pack a punch,” BoM meteorologist Angus Hines said on Saturday.

The storms are expected to impact Melbourne, parts of Gippsland, the north-eastern ranges, and north-central Victoria, with damaging winds the greatest risk.

The risk area will extend further north through inland NSW into the evening – up to Queensland’s southern interior and along the NSW coast south of Sydney around Wollongong and the Illawarra.

The forecast in these areas includes possible damaging winds, heavy rainfall and large hailstones.

“Expecting some very active storms here a little bit later on in the day, mid to late afternoon for many of these areas, and potentially not until the evening hours by the time we’re looking at storms getting out towards the east coast,” Hines said.

The focus of concern will shift further north on Sunday, with heavy rain and storms around Brisbane during the afternoon and early evening.

Severe thunderstorms were most likely for parts of the NSW mid-north coast, the northern rivers, parts of the tablelands and the Hunter region, with possible hail, heavy rainfall, flash flooding and destructive winds of more than 125km/h.

Areas that had recorded heightened rainfall in the past fortnight were also at risk of flash flooding, Hines said.

“If you do live through this area, tomorrow is definitely a day you’ll want to keep a watch on the radar to see if any big storms are headed your way,” he said.

A broader area of potential concern for Sunday stretches from Newcastle, north of Sydney, up to Gympie on the Sunshine Coast.

A severe wind warning is also in place across the mountains of northern Victoria and southern NSW, with wind gusts of more than 100km/h recorded on Saturday morning.

articles.title: Eight in 10 homes in London’s poshest postcodes now sell below asking price, Coutts finds
articles.excerpt:
Sellers in areas such as Belgravia and Mayfair face hundreds of thousands of pounds in losses as property prices fall

Eight out of 10 properties in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods – such as Ma...
articles.body_text:
Sellers in areas such as Belgravia and Mayfair face hundreds of thousands of pounds in losses as property prices fall

Eight out of 10 properties in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods – such as Mayfair, Belgravia and Knightsbridge – now sell below asking price, according to research by Coutts, which provides private banking services to wealthy clients.

Property prices in “prime central London”, which covers the city’s most expensive postcodes, have dropped 5% in the third quarter of 2026, as the slowdown in the UK’s property market hits its wealthiest residents.

It means some affluent people are facing hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of pounds in losses to the value of their homes, with properties selling at an average 10% discount to their asking price, Coutts found.

Prices in the highest end of London’s property market are now 14% below their peak in 2014, having been hit hard by Brexit, the Covid pandemic, higher property taxes and a surge in borrowing costs. Buying and selling agents in the capital have also reported a slowdown in interest from foreign-born buyers after the abolition of the non-dom tax regime.

Exclusive areas such as Knightsbridge and Belgravia, and South Kensington have been hit the hardest, Coutts said, with prices 30.8% and 26.9% below their peaks respectively.

Alex Webster, head of lending at the bank, said buyers and sellers at the top end of the market were taking a more cautious approach, even before the chancellor, John Healey’s, first budget this week.

Sellers will now be watching to see if the budget “encourages some of that delayed activity to return”, she said. “But financing conditions and the wider economic environment will continue to influence the market.”

There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since last December but volatility in the bond market has driven up the swap rates that influence the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages.

While the Bank of England has kept its key interest rate on hold at 3.75%, expectations are growing that next week its monetary policy committee will vote to increase the rate for the first time in three years to 4%.

In the meantime, sellers in prime central London are increasingly shying away, Coutts found, with new listings down 14% compared with the previous quarter and available stock down by 6% year-on-year.

Transactions were 9.1% lower in the third quarter of this year, it said, with the biggest slowdown in the £2m-£5m band, where transactions were down 22.3%.

However, separate research from the estate agent Savills found that buyers at the very top end of the market are driving activity, with 26 transactions above £10m in the third quarter of this year, taking the total to 127 over the past year. Together, these sales were worth £2.88bn, it found.

articles.title: ‘Reparations now’: King and Burnham face protests at Antigua Commonwealth summit
articles.excerpt:
Activists see meeting as opportunity to demand UK confront role in transatlantic enslavement

“The royal family enslaved us! Apologise now! Reparatory justice now!”

King Charles and the UK prime mini...
articles.body_text:
Activists see meeting as opportunity to demand UK confront role in transatlantic enslavement

“The royal family enslaved us! Apologise now! Reparatory justice now!”

King Charles and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, will be greeted with messages as they travel through Antigua’s capital, St John’s, to attend meetings at the Commonwealth leaders’ summit next week. On billboards, placards and T-shirts, in letters and at a candlelight vigil for the thousands of Africans trafficked to Antigua and Barbuda during the transatlantic slave trade, the message from the Caribbean will be pervasive: slavery reparations is not an issue they “are going to be able to dodge”.

James Knight of Citizens for Reparatory Justice, which is organising some of the demonstrations, said the king and UK government had made protest necessary.

“It is definitely necessary that we make known our deep sense of indignation in response to what has been announced ahead of the meeting by the British government and King Charles that there will be no apology, no reparations,” he said, “and to make that announcement when you’re coming to a meeting where people have been asking to have the matter discussed, to us, is extremely insulting [and] insensitive”.

On Friday, Burnham went further than any previous British prime minister in an article for the Guardian, writing: “We are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade. Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them.” While that does not pass the threshold that Knight set out, it will be viewed by some as a significant development.

The Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm), usually a collegial gathering of leaders from the bloc’s 56 member countries, will be surrounded by reparations events. Though outside the official agenda, protests, a beach vigil to remember the enslaved and the launch of a “global reparations caravan” – described by organisers as an international movement combining reparations advocacy, demonstrations and culture – are intended to ensure the issue is difficult to ignore.

For campaigners, this Chogm is the culmination of more than a decade of calls from Caribbean leaders for Britain to acknowledge its role in the enslavement of millions of Africans and the colonisation of African and Caribbean countries, and to address the enduring consequences.

Last week, the chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom) reparations commission, Hilary Beckles, emphasised that the absence of a dedicated official event did not mean reparations would remain peripheral. He described the gathering as “the Chogm of reparations” and the “first round of reparations negotiations”.

“This is the meeting of the Commonwealth in the Caribbean, and the number one item in the Caribbean as far as this gathering is concerned is reparatory justice,” Beckles said.

The Guardian understands that organisations and groups supporting the reparations movement, including representatives from the Repair Campaign, the UK law firm Leigh Day, the Open Society Foundations, the African philanthropic organisation TrustAfrica and the UK’s all-party parliamentary group for Afrikan reparations, will get together outside the main meeting to discuss the issue. Caribbean leaders are also expected to push the issue during closed-door meetings.

But while the reparations movement views the summit as a potential turning point, successive British prime ministers have maintained that the UK will not pay slavery reparations, a position Burnham stuck to in his article, writing: “I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs”.

The Caricom reparations commission has also revealed that the Caribbean was unable to secure unanimous Commonwealth agreement for foreign ministers to advance discussions on historical harms from the transatlantic slave trade through “structured, inclusive, and good faith dialogue”.

Meanwhile, Buckingham Palace has sought to draw a line between the monarch and government policy. In a letter, seen by the Guardian, to the ambassador Dorbrene O’Marde, the chair of the Antigua and Barbuda reparations support commission, the palace said questions relating to the UK’s position on reparations were for the British government. The response followed a letter from O’Marde describing “blanket ‘no apologies’ statements from both government and monarchy” as “shameful” and a refusal to accept historical responsibility.

O’Marde said that despite strong declarations about the suffering caused by slavery and the monarch’s own calls for conversation and acknowledgment of the past, there had been no progression towards action. Instead, he said, the UK appeared to rely on “verbal gymnastics” to avoid an apology. “They’re all schooled not to make an apology,” he said.

But for O’Marde, the obstacles are unlikely to withstand the growing tide of international support for reparations, including a UN resolution in March describing the trafficking and racialised chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity. The resolution was backed by 123 countries. Reparations, he said, now had a sound legal and political backbone that made progress increasingly plausible.

In September, Jamaican officials lodged a landmark petition to the king seeking legal advice on its claim for slavery reparations, which will be heard by the privy council in March.

Verene Shepherd, the vice-chair of the Caricom reparations commission, who was involved in drafting the 25 March UN resolution and an August recommendation from the UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (Cerd), said the developments reiterated that “crime does not rot”.

Shepherd said Cerd’s recommendation that countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination was “grounded in international law and historical evidence” about slavery and colonisation and their continuing impact. She described it as “a concrete step towards remedying historical wrongs against Africans and people of African descent”.

“As far as former colonists and Africans are concerned, a crime does not rot. It is carried forward until justice is achieved,” she said, adding that Cerd’s involvement “certainly strengthens the movement’s international legitimacy”.

Central to that campaign is an apology. The Caricom reparations commission’s manifesto and 10-point plan, which sets out what it describes as the “moral, ethical and legal case for reparations” for the enslavement of African people, puts a “full and formal apology” first.

For Shepherd, its importance lies in accepting responsibility. “It would accept responsibility for these crimes, commit to non-repetition and pledge to repair the harms caused to the victims and their descendants, the men, the women, the children harmed by chattel enslavement. It would represent an ethical and legal acknowledgment of how present inequalities and racial injustices are rooted in the history of such criminal conduct,” she said.

O’Marde said an apology would create a pathway towards what the Caribbean ultimately wants: fruitful negotiations with the UK on reparations.

But among Caribbean citizens there is still scepticism over whether even that would be enough. In Guyana, where the king visited on Thursday and Friday, Ron ChangYuen, a visual designer, said unless the king could shift the reparations conversation towards “actual results in some significant way”, he saw little point in the visit.

Deandra Daniels, however, said an apology alone would not satisfy her. “Getting the king to say sorry isn’t enough because we have generational trauma,” the dramatist said. “We expect him as a king of a dynasty that was built on the back of my ancestors to do much more.”

Inside the reparations movement, however, there is optimism that Antigua could move the campaign forward.

“I’m sure at the end of this meeting, there will be something more advanced going forward because it is not an issue that they are going to be able to dodge. And this is the point of the protest, to make sure that they are not able to dodge this issue over and over again,” said Knight.

articles.title: Is time up for backyard fireworks? UK ministers weigh partial ban over noise concerns
articles.excerpt:
Consultation follows growing calls from campaigners, vets and National Farmers’ Union for tighter regulation

As the nights draw in, the season of sparklers begins, with Diwali, Bonfire Night and New ...
articles.body_text:
Consultation follows growing calls from campaigners, vets and National Farmers’ Union for tighter regulation

As the nights draw in, the season of sparklers begins, with Diwali, Bonfire Night and New Year’s Eve among the occasions typically celebrated with fireworks. But if campaigners get their way, this could be the last blast for bangers in the back yard.

In January concerns about the noise and availability of fireworks were aired in a parliamentary debate, with two petitions clocking up more than 180,000 signatures each, while earlier this month the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade closed a consultation on proposals including making louder fireworks only available to professional users.

Harriet Main, a public affairs manager at the RSPCA, said the charity was thrilled by the consultation: “For too long, pets, wildlife, and livestock have suffered from stress, fright and severe injury caused by loud unregulated back-yard DIY displays.

“Public appetite for change is overwhelming: the RSPCA hosted its own online action to help supporters submit their views to the consultation, and this generated over 51,000 responses eager to speak up for animals. This extraordinary turnout demonstrates just how deeply people across Britain care about protecting animals from the devastating impacts of unnecessarily loud fireworks.”

In recent years there have been reports of a host of animal fatalities linked to fireworks, from the death of a baby red panda at Edinburgh zoo to a dachshund in North Yorkshire.

Ministers have ruled out a complete ban on the public buying fireworks. Instead, their proposals include expanding the list of fireworks banned for general sale and reducing the permitted decibel level of consumer fireworks from 120dB to 110dB, meaning their loudness would be approximately halved.

Dr Gwen Rees, the president of the British Veterinary Association, said vets were acutely aware of the fear, distress, injury and lasting anxiety fireworks caused to animals in the UK each year. “Lower noise limits would reduce one of the main causes of firework-related distress while allowing celebrations to continue,” she said. “But quieter fireworks are not a complete solution. Flashes and unpredictable timing can still affect animals, so clearer labelling, responsible use, tighter controls on sales and private use, and better public awareness are also essential to protect animal welfare.”

A tightening of regulations has been backed by organisations including the National Farmers’ Union, which has cited animal welfare concerns and fire risks in relation to private firework displays. “One member reported losing around four acres of wheat after a firework landed in a standing crop during harvest,” the NFU noted.

Changes to pyrotechnics and fireworks regulations will be made as soon as parliamentary time allows after analysis of the feedback from the consultation, the government said, adding that there would be a six-month “transitional period” after the law was changed.

However, the British Fireworks Assocation has pushed back, noting that many of the behaviours that frustrate communities – such as setting off fireworks in a public place or after 1am – are already illegal, and that removing large numbers of legal and regulated products from the consumer market might push people towards finding hidden-market fireworks and pyrotechnics.

Recent efforts to tackle the use of fireworks and pyrotechnics in Scotland – including the introduction of “firework control zones” where the devices are banned – have had a mixed reception.

Helen Whitelegg, the campaigns manager at the charity Redwings Horse Sanctuary, said: “We believe the zones create a two-tier system of protection where they are put in place and risk pushing more use of fireworks to the surrounding areas.”

She added: “We are aware that the widely anticipated step of introducing a licencing requirement for anyone using fireworks has been shelved due to lack of resources and there is no indication when this part of the legislation is likely to be brought in.”

But it is not only the UK where firework fervour has cooled. In the Netherlands a countrywide ban on most consumer fireworks came into effect in August, while Czechia has also tightened its regulations. On 29 November, Swiss citzens will have their say on proposals to ban noisy fireworks.

In Germany, there is already a limited window in which fireworks can be bought or used, while there are also bans on fireworks in some zones and near certain facilities. Even then, there are calls for stronger regulations, with one survey suggesting almost half of those polled were in favour of a total ban, with exceptions only for very small fireworks such as sparklers.

Whitelegg said that among other measures, Redwings backed a reduction in the maximum loudness of fireworks to 90dB, as is the case in New Zealand, noting that while a Dutch-style ban would be preferable, the use of low-noise fireworks presented a practical compromise.

“I think the direction of travel does suggest that change is inevitable,” she said. “And because of what we’re seeing in other countries, it’s not unique to the UK by any stretch of the imagination.”

articles.title: Federal judge blocks Trump DOJ threats against election workers ahead of 2026 midterms
articles.excerpt:
A federal judge barred the Trump administration from threatening election workers with prosecution over suspected noncitizen ballots, citing likely voting rights violations days before the midterms.

...
articles.body_text:
A federal judge barred the Trump administration from threatening election workers with prosecution over suspected noncitizen ballots, citing likely voting rights violations days before the midterms.

A federal judge on Friday temporarily barred the Trump administration from threatening election workers with criminal prosecution over ballots tied to suspected noncitizens.

U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson found that the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security likely violated the Voting Rights Act's prohibition against voter intimidation by threatening election workers with prosecution for processing ballots from voters the administration claims are ineligible, just days before the midterm elections.

"One of the hallmarks of a fair election is the freedom to exercise the right to vote free from threat, fear, or intimidation," Thompson, a Biden-appointed judge, wrote in the eight-page order.

The ruling comes as the Trump administration has sought voter registration information from states ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, arguing that its efforts are aimed at preventing noncitizen voting and protecting election integrity.

BIDEN-APPOINTED JUDGE BLOCKS VOTER-FRAUD PROBES IN BATTLEGROUND STATES JUST DAYS BEFORE MIDTERMS

Election workers sort ballots during early voting ahead of the midterm election at City Hall in San Francisco, California, on Oct. 21, 2026. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The temporary restraining order prohibits federal officials from threatening, intimidating or coercing state and local election workers into halting ballot processing solely because the administration alleges certain registered voters are ineligible.

The order also bars the administration from demanding that election officials remove registered voters from voter rolls, refuse to issue them ballots or segregate or decline to count their ballots based solely on those allegations.

The lawsuit was brought by labor unions and civil rights organizations, including the Service Employees International Union and the NAACP.

"Because the public has a paramount interest in ensuring that election officials and workers are able to carry out their work in accordance with federal law and election procedure, and the official day of the Elections is only a couple of days away, the balance of the equities and public interest weigh in Plaintiffs' favor," Thompson wrote.

"Ballots have already been issued," Thompson also noted. "Americans have already begun voting."

NINTH CIRCUIT QUESTIONS TRUMP DOJ'S EMERGENCY REQUEST TO SET ASIDE 20,000 CALIFORNIA MAIL BALLOTS

President Donald Trump's administration was temporarily barred by a federal judge from threatening election workers with criminal prosecution over ballots tied to suspected noncitizens. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Thompson also ordered the administration to notify state and local governments that received the disputed letters that the demands and threats of prosecution contained in them have been blocked.

Earlier Friday, a federal appeals court separately ruled against the Trump administration's emergency request to require California to set aside mail-in ballots associated with roughly 20,000 voters federal officials identified as likely noncitizens while their citizenship status was verified.

The Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals denied the Justice Department's request to set aside the disputed mail-in ballots while officials reviewed the voters' citizenship status, handing the administration another setback just four days before Election Day.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

An election official sorts ballots during early voting, Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025, in Portland, Maine. (Robert F. Bukaty/AP)

Fox News Digital's Jasmine Baehr and Reuters contributed to this report.

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

articles.title: After the ‘martyr’s’ funeral: The families left behind by Yemen’s war
articles.excerpt: Sanaa, Yemen – Pickups carrying the bodies of Houthi fighters occasionally travel through the streets of Sanaa. Alongside them in the back, gunmen accompany the fallen fighters on their final journey ...
articles.body_text:
Sanaa, Yemen – Pickups carrying the bodies of Houthi fighters occasionally travel through the streets of Sanaa. Alongside them in the back, gunmen accompany the fallen fighters on their final journey to the cemetery.

A song known as “Our martyrs are our greats” echoes loudly from the moving vehicles, drawing the attention of passersby. At the cemetery, mourners solemnly pay their respects to the fallen fighters and show solidarity with their families.

Funerals of fighters have been a recurring sight in Yemen over the past few weeks.

Earlier this month, the Yemeni government said its forces killed or wounded 1,540 Houthis in 24 hours. Last week, the government said 16,100 Houthi operatives and commanders had been killed or wounded since October 5.

Houthis have also killed hundreds of pro-government troops over the past few weeks, with an October 19 missile attack on a security camp in Shabwa killing more than 70 government soldiers.

While the families of the deceased fighters receive fleeting public tributes at cemeteries, their grief and loss endure long after the funerals. For them, life has become more difficult, economic hardships have deepened and sorrow is a constant companion.

“The martyrdom of my brother, Abdulaziz, on October 10 broke us and robbed us of peace of mind. We could smile to hide our pain, but our hearts are filled with bottomless grief,” Akram, a 23-year-old resident of Sanaa, told Al Jazeera.

Abdulaziz, 21, was killed in Dhubab, in southwestern Yemen, while fighting alongside the Houthi group, two months after being recruited, Akram said.

Before Abdulaziz went to the front line, the two brothers worked in Sanaa as daily-wage workers in construction or agriculture. When they managed to get work, they pooled their earnings to cover the living expenses of their six-member family. That made the family’s financial difficulties “manageable”, said Akram.

Today, he struggles without his brother and covering the family’s basic needs has become a harder task.

“I lost my pillar of strength, Abdulaziz. His income, along with mine, used to cover water, electricity and food expenses. Without him, I am like a bird with one wing, burdened by so many responsibilities,” said Akram.

Over the past few days, petrol and diesel prices have risen by 10 percent in Houthi-controlled northwestern Yemen, adding to the cost of basic goods and increasing pressure on struggling families, such as Akram’s.

“When it comes to paying the fees for water, electricity, or buying groceries, it does not matter if your relative is a martyr or not. You have to pay or starve to death,” said Akram.

In recent months, Yemen has faced a major escalation in fighting between Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-aligned Houthi group that controls parts of the country.

The latest escalation “threatens to be absolutely devastating” for food security, said the World Food Programme’s Assistant Executive Director for Programme Operations, Matthew Hollingworth, earlier this month.

“We are looking at a hunger crisis that is going to grow as it persists,” Hollingworth added.

The Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in September 2014 and subsequently took control of much of northern and western Yemen. Since then, the conflict has remained unresolved.

Like many other deceased fighters’ families in Houthi-controlled areas, Houthi authorities gave Akram’s family a food basket, which included flour, cooking oil, rice and sugar.

However, the supply of food or financial assistance is irregular, Sanaa-based Ali Yahia, a 55-year-old father of a deceased fighter, told Al Jazeera.

“My son was killed four years ago on the Saudi-Yemen border when he was fighting for the Sanaa-based government. Since then, I have received food baskets at different times. Sometimes, I receive them twice a year or thrice a year, or four times a year,” he said.

For Yahia, this support is insufficient, and he argues that “fair compensation” would be a monthly salary of $200 at least. “This amount of money would help a family cover the basics each month,” he said.

Yahia has two other sons who support him. One is a delivery rider in Sanaa and the other works at a restaurant.

“With their support, my living conditions have improved. But if a family depends on a fighter’s income, the death of the fighter sparks a living and psychological ordeal for the whole family,” he said.

According to the World Food Programme, 18.3 million people across Yemen face severe food insecurity, while 2.2 million children under five suffer from acute malnutrition.

As the number of fighters killed on the front lines rises, the authorities’ ability to support bereaved families is increasingly stretched, Ali Mohammed, a Houthi representative in Sanaa, told Al Jazeera.

“Martyrs today are too many and their families deserve due support. However, the rising number of martyrs affects the level of support they receive. Assistance is distributed so that every family gets some,” said Mohammed.

He argued that the “complete Houthi victory will lead to stability in the country and this will give authorities a better opportunity to look after the families of the martyrs.” He added: “This will take time”.

On October 25, the Sanaa-based Houthi Ministry of Youth and Sports commemorated Martyrs’ Day in the presence of many Houthi officials.

During the event, the group’s Undersecretary for the Sports Sector, Ali Hadban, emphasised the importance of observing the occasion to “draw inspiration from the lessons of sacrifice and selflessness, and to reflect on the enduring legacies of the martyrs who defended the nation”.

He noted that the victories achieved across various fronts are the direct result of the sacrifices made by “these noble martyrs”, emphasising the need to provide support and care for their families.

At the end of 2021, the UN estimated that 377,000 people had been killed directly or indirectly by the war in Yemen. The recent return of fighting has claimed more lives.

Adel Dashela, researcher at the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, described the public celebration of fallen fighters as “an alien practice” that emerged during the war.

“This practice reflects the normalisation of violence and encourages children to risk their lives and die under various sectarian and political slogans. Yemenis did not witness this phenomenon until the Houthi group took control of the capital, Sanaa,” Dashela told Al Jazeera.

Families may be encouraged to participate in these rituals and may find themselves compelled to do so under social and political pressure, he said. “The reality, however, is that public displays of honour do not alleviate families’ suffering. Instead, the social, psychological and financial consequences of their loss remain their burden to bear.”

In many cases, women and children assume responsibility for supporting their families after the death of the breadwinner.

“Thus, women and children bear the real cost of these losses, while public celebrations remain detached from their everyday realities and the ongoing suffering of bereaved families,” Dashela added.

articles.title: Spain train disaster clouds Sánchez chances of re-election
articles.excerpt:
The breaking news from Spain this week was shocking but also shockingly familiar: another collision on the high-speed rail line south from Madrid, with reports of dozens killed.

It is just nine month...
articles.body_text:
The breaking news from Spain this week was shocking but also shockingly familiar: another collision on the high-speed rail line south from Madrid, with reports of dozens killed.

It is just nine months since two trains crashed near Cordoba, killing 46 people. Now 69 bodies have been recovered here in central Spain, from wreckage strewn over the tracks and down an embankment.

For the victims' families it is devastating; a personal tragedy.

But it is also a national disaster that has shattered confidence in the country's rail network and the Socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez. It is playing out just weeks before the snap general election he called.

Pedro Sánchez was already facing public anger over alleged corruption and housing costs

The formal investigation into the Toledo train disaster has only just been launched but the government has been quick to take control of the narrative.

From the first hours after the collision, Transport Minister Oscar Puente began suggesting "human error" was to blame, batting responsibility as far as possible from the cabinet.

On Friday, he appeared before the press for a second time to set out what he called the "objective facts" of the crash and counter a surge of criticism against the government.

The opposition People's Party (PP) is among those calling for his resignation as a "moral" and "ethical" move.

Instead after expressing "huge pain and sadness" for the victims, Puente went on the offensive.

He rejected talk of chronic underinvestment in infrastructure and insisted that Spain's high-speed signalling safety system, the LZB, was neither old nor inadequate: Germany and Austria use the same.

In Spain, it has already failed 170 times so far this year, he revealed, but called that "normal" and around the EU average.

The problem surrounds what happens next - when the system fails and control of the line shifts to manual.

In this case, the minister highlighted a series of human errors that proved catastrophic.

Listen: Audio recordings between train driver and controller

Crucially, at one point a controller instructed a stalled train to restart, clearing it to advance at up to 160km/h (100 mph) even though a second train was stuck on the line up ahead.

The impending collision was clear from audio calls and on big screens in the control centre in Madrid.

"They worked. We checked. They could see what was happening," Puente confirmed. But the advancing train was never ordered to stop.

"I'm no judge... But these are the facts."

So would he take personal and political responsibility anyway, and resign? Puente called it his "duty", rather, to remain as minister.

"I'll face up to things, explain, elucidate," he countered. "I'll think how to improve the system, and give confidence to those who want to travel by train and feel calm and safe."

But Spaniards will take a lot of persuading.

"This is not only a very serious accident, but the second in a very short time," Paco Camas of the pollster Ipsos points out.

An investigation into January's crash in Adamuz, near Cordoba, is still open, with initial reports suggesting there was a crack in the rails -  very different to the latest collision.

"It destroys people's confidence not only in the railways but institutions in general," Camas warns. "And in Spain when such things happen, we know that people blame their government."

For Team Sánchez it is the latest in a spiral of crises.

Allegations of corruption against the prime minister's close relatives still persist, all denied.

Then there was a sudden influx of migrants from Morocco this summer to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. That got right-wing opponents shouting about incompetence and underfunding.

Later, a video of a pensioner being forcibly evicted from her home went viral and sparked street protests.

That's when Sánchez called an early election.

His chances of winning the vote looked slim even before the train crash. Now they have plummeted.

The death of Maricarmen Abascal, evicted from her home of more than 70 years, sparked widespread housing protests across Spain

Most recent polls showed the centre-right PP coming first and forming a coalition with the far-right Vox.

"They have this majority in almost 95% of the simulations we have done," Prof Pablo Simon of Madrid's Carlos III University explains.

But Sánchez had been running a positive campaign, trying to lure apathetic voters to the polls to vote socialist.

"They've totally lost control of the agenda and the emotion of this campaign," Simon says. "It's going to be extremely difficult now. There is this general mood of decay, of a country that's not working properly. A depression."

There have already been small protests over the train crash led by far-right groups in Madrid and large numbers of police are on stand-by this weekend ahead of further potential clashes, organised online.

"We all travelled in silence and really sad," Paloma told me at the city station, where she had just pulled in on a half empty train.

She admitted she's scared of the high-speed network now and angry at the government.

"This crash will change all of our votes, completely," Paloma said. "We'll shift from the left wing to the right. Because of everything that's happened."

Lucia takes the high-speed AVE into Madrid each day, and is scared too.

"This was human error. But there's been two accidents now with more than 100 dead," she says. "Things here are really bad. They have to change."

Producer Davide Ghiglione contributed to this report

articles.title: Why are US, Russia and China racing to put nuclear reactors on the moon?
articles.excerpt:
The United States, Russia and China are racing to build nuclear reactors on the moon, as scientists warn about the possible risk of a radioactive mishap.

In January, NASA, the US space agency, announ...
articles.body_text:
The United States, Russia and China are racing to build nuclear reactors on the moon, as scientists warn about the possible risk of a radioactive mishap.

In January, NASA, the US space agency, announced plans to develop a nuclear reactor on the moon by the end of 2030. Russia, working with China, aims to do the same by 2036 as they strive to advance space exploration.

The reactors will be needed to power mining of frozen water trapped deep in the moon’s craters, which scientists believe could supply drinking water, air, and rocket fuel for future bases. The reactors would also provide power for lunar bases.

The US said NASA’s Lunar Reactor 1 would produce 20 kilowatts of electricity, creating enough power to run on its own for five years without maintenance.

NASA’s reactor is designed to be compact, weighing under 6,000kg (13,200 lbs) and will fit inside a rocket compartment measuring 3.7 metres (12 feet) long by 5.5 metres (18 ft) wide.

Russia is also building a nuclear reactor, which is expected to produce 10 kilowatts. The reactor, called Selena, will be able to run for a decade without maintenance. It will be ready to power a Chinese-led moon base by about 2036.

The Selena reactor is expected to be even lighter than NASA’s, weighing about 1,100 to 1,300kg (2,400 to 2,800 lbs) for an easier and softer landing on the lunar surface.

This would not be the first time nuclear reactors have been placed in outer space.

The Soviet Union launched more than 30 nuclear fission reactors into Earth’s orbit between the late 1960s and the 1980s to power spy satellites during the Cold War.

The small, 1,000kg (2,200 lbs) reactors powered radar-tracking spy satellites using heat from splitting uranium atoms into 3 to 5 kilowatts of electricity. They are no longer operational, and no other country has sent nuclear reactors into space.

The US has spent $20bn on advanced space nuclear programmes over the past 70 years, but has never successfully launched a nuclear reactor into space since an experiment in 1965.

That experiment was carried out to see if nuclear energy could power a satellite. It worked at first but accidentally shut down after just 43 days because a non-nuclear electrical part of the satellite broke down. It is still floating up in space today.

Previous attempts by the US to develop nuclear projects have stalled due to shifting budget priorities.

First, scientists will have to build a reactor on Earth, which will then be transported to the moon using a robotic spacecraft that fires rocket engines for a slow and gentle touchdown.

Both the US and Russia say they would keep their reactors switched off until they reach the moon, to keep radioactive risk at a minimum until the last step.

Once set up on the moon, the reactors would be designed to run without maintenance for years, supplying power to bases engaged in mining on the lunar surface.

The US, China and Russia want to build bases near the moon’s south pole, close to the known sources of water ice. The ice sits in the permanently shadowed craters, where sunlight has not reached for millions of years.

As well as powering the moon bases, the reactors would also supply enough power for mining. So far, the US, Russia and China want to mine for frozen water which, once released, could be used to support life on the moon at bases where people could live and conduct research.

Tech billionaire Elon Musk has also said he wants to extract minerals such as aluminium, titanium, and silicon, required for manufacturing satellites.

Solar power for such endeavours would be limited as the sun shines on any one spot on the moon only half the time, so solar panels would go dark for about two weeks every month.

Simon Middleburgh, director of Bangor University’s Nuclear Futures Institute (NFI), told Al Jazeera that solar power is too limited to provide the steady flow of energy a moon base would need, while batteries and diesel are too costly, because everything has to be launched from Earth.

Nuclear energy is the “obvious choice”, Middleburgh said, adding that it must be used “responsibly”.

It is likely that three or four reactors working together would be required to provide sufficient energy for mining lunar ice as well as supporting a moon base, he added.

In a December 2025 executive order, US President Donald Trump ordered NASA to build a lunar reactor ready to launch by 2030. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin have revealed similar plans.

In August this year, Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said the US is in a “race to the moon, in a race with China”.

Middleburgh said the 2030 deadline is likely for building the reactor itself, but the harder part will be landing on the moon and safely setting up the system.

“The biggest challenge isn’t really the nuclear technology at all; it is the regulation for launch, the availability of a launch platform itself, and the landing and setting up the system on the lunar surface ready for it to be operated sustainably and safely,” he said.

The race to the moon also comes amid growing military competition beyond Earth. In September, the US announced it had deployed weapons into orbit, which officials said would be used to defend US forces.

While the US did not provide details about these “weapons”, experts say they are likely to be space-based communications jammers, rather than kinetic ones that launch strikes.

The announcement raised concerns about the concept of “space weapons” or the use of space for military purposes, including the potential targeting of satellites that provide GPS, communications and intelligence.

Middleburgh told Al Jazeera that an accident during the launch of the reactors would be less frightening than it sounds because uranium alone, before it is used in a reactor, is not very radioactive. However, that changes once the reactor is switched on.

The risk is bigger if a running reactor falls back onto Earth, analysts say.

In 1978, a Soviet satellite carrying a reactor, Kosmos 954, scattered radioactive material across nearly 124,300 square km (48,000sq miles) of northern Canada.

The accident forced an expensive military cleanup of the highly radioactive fragments and microscopic particles.

On the moon, Middleburgh says, any contaminated area would be “extremely localised” if there were to be a similar accident.

Legally, no one. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans countries from “claiming” the moon or any part of it, though they have ownership of the equipment they send there. The treaty does not ban nuclear power in space.

Antonino Salmeri, director of the Lunar Policy Platform, a nonprofit, told Al Jazeera that a reactor can be lawful if it follows the treaty’s principles, including peaceful use and avoiding harmful contamination.

Norbert Schorghofer, a senior scientist at the Planetary Science Institute in Arizona, US, told Al Jazeera all signatories “have the right to mine the lunar surface as long as it is for peaceful purposes”.

Whichever country’s reactor gets to the “best” water ice first could claim a “safety zone”, which would not be a land claim but could operate like one. Salmeri said declaring one creates no territorial rights, but a reactor shuts others out anyway, because nobody wants to enter a radioactive area.

A Lunar Policy Platform report released last month points to another problem: Who is responsible if something goes wrong? The report says existing liability rules have not been designed to regulate the use of long-term hazardous equipment on another celestial body.
